articles.title: After 5 years, Wasp 1.0 is coming: a 6-month plan for our full-stack JS framework
articles.description: The time has come: Wasp 1.0 is now officially in the works! ETA: ~6 months.  Even though still...
articles.body_html:
The time has come: Wasp 1.0 is now officially in the works! ETA: ~6 months.

Even though still young in framework-years, Wasp has been around for some time now (>5y), with over 100 releases, user stories ranging from startups to Fortune 500 companies, $5M raised in funding so far, and a team of currently 8 people and growing behind it plus all the awesome people from our community (waspeteers).

And yet, for years now, we kept Wasp in Beta. Read on to learn why, what changed, and what you can expect from 1.0.

Want an email when Wasp 1.0 lands? Subscribe here.

The freedom of Beta

For a long time, we didn't have an exact set of features in mind that would allow us to say Wasp is now 1.0.

We always knew what we wanted though, and believed we would recognize it when we got there: the "fullstackiest", managed experience of building web apps there is.
The experience of writing only the code you care about, at the level of detail you want, and the rest being taken care of for you.
All expressed purely in code, flexible, free and easy to deploy anywhere.

That led us to some unconventional choices when designing Wasp:

  • We designed our own custom declarative language for describing a web app at a high level (the "Spec") and its own custom compiler. (psst, that was a bit of a mistake though).
  • Our definition of "full-stack" is broader than usual for JS frameworks, fully capturing frontend, backend, database, and deployment, and really everything that falls in between.
  • Even though it is currently based on React + Node + Prisma, the underlying machinery has always been designed to allow adding support for other stacks in the future, in large part thanks to the aforementioned Spec and compiler.

Being in Beta gave us the freedom to explore all these concepts unhindered by the weight and responsibility of maintaining a >=1.0 version of a framework (although we did end up following a lot of "production" practices already in Beta: looking at you, brave people who couldn't be stopped from deploying to production).

Ready for 1.0

What makes Wasp ready for 1.0 now? After all this time, I dare say the picture crystallized into something much clearer.

  • We found the right shape for the "Spec" (went from our custom language to TypeScript) without giving up on our vision (this was a big one!).
  • We developed an intuition for how to balance managed experience with flexibility.
  • We collected a lot of feedback on all the major features of Wasp (Auth, RPC, Jobs, Routing, API, Entities, Deployment, etc) and know what people care about and how to get there.
  • We are now fully committed to bringing the Full Stack Modules to life, the crown of the "fullstackiest" experience we are aiming for.

We can now see the exact road, paved with GitHub issues, to Wasp 1.0, and it feels right.

The roadmap

You can check the exact roadmap on GitHub.
It consists of epics, and each of those further develops into sub-epics and specific issues.

Roughly, we can break down the epics in the roadmap into:

  • General polish (DX).
  • Rework of core features (Routing, Auth, RPC, etc).
  • Production readiness work (core deps policy, perf/scaling docs, native Win support, etc).
  • Novel features (Full Stack Modules, RBAC, etc).

General polish (DX)

While in Beta, we focused a lot on innovating and testing different ideas, and often prioritized those over the rough edges.

However, when accumulated, rough edges become annoying, so one big class of tasks for 1.0 is a lot of smaller, targeted improvements, mostly DX focused.

Some of these are: making Wasp work better with agent orchestrators, nicer output in the terminal, nicer docs, faster npm install, etc.

Check Epic #2884 for more details.

Rework of core features

We never lacked ideas on how to make each of the core Wasp features better (Auth, RPC, Jobs, Email Sender, WebSockets, API, Deployment, etc), but for many of these it was hard to prioritize them while working on bigger framework-spanning improvements (e.g. Spec).

For 1.0, we will bring each of these to a new level! Most of the ideas are already written down in a lot of detail in related GitHub issues, and while some features will require only a smaller touch-up, some will go through a major rework.

For example, Auth will move away from Lucia and add highly requested features like account merging, 2FA, magic links, passkeys, etc. Also, as it currently stands, we will almost certainly reshape it into a more modular implementation that will, next to Wasp Auth, allow using BetterAuth, Clerk, WorkOS or any other auth provider that can implement our auth interface.

Another big one is Deployment: we are looking to simplify wasp build to produce a single server, which will unlock many other things. We are also exploring the smoothest option out there for free hosting of Wasp apps and will be adding it as one of the options in our one-command deploy: wasp deploy <provider>, while also making the current options (Fly, Railway) more robust.

For a full list, see the major features planned for 1.0 in our roadmap.”

Production readiness work

These are non-feature-specific tasks related to bringing Wasp to the level we expect from a >=1.0 framework.

A big one is the core deps policy: from 1.0 onwards we will have a strict policy on how current we keep our core deps (e.g. never more than 6 months behind the latest, which keeps us up to date while avoiding bleeding-edge hiccups).

Then there are docs on performance and scaling: while a lot of this just comes down to the underlying stack (React, Node, Prisma), some of it is also Wasp specific, and we want to make it very clear and easy to understand what you can expect from Wasp in this regard.

And also native Windows support! Wasp works on WSL on Windows, but having it run directly on Windows is something you would expect from a 1.0 framework, right?

Check Epic #2888 for more details.

Novel features

And finally, we are not giving up on innovating just because we are closing in on 1.0.

The star here is FSMs (Full Stack Modules): the ability to define and distribute modular, vertical slices of your web app, e.g. Stripe payments, file upload, AI chat, etc. Imagine libraries, but frontend + backend + database + Spec + even deployment in the future, all type-safe and configurable. It's something we are extremely excited about and have been slowly preparing for quite some time now. We wrote more about the idea in JavaScript still can't ship a full-stack module.

FSMs might not sound like a 1.0 thing right off the bat, but we see them becoming so integral to how Wasp apps will be built that we want to have them, and their effects on Wasp's API, in place before 1.0.

By the way, we are open to ideas for a better name since LLMs keep thinking we are talking about Finite State Machines.

And then we have some more exciting ideas (well, popular requests really) like RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), a modular database layer that would allow support for Drizzle, Wasp Studio (visual representation of your codebase + Wasp dev tooling), etc.
These are more of a stretch goal and might or might not yet be fully stable in 1.0, but we would love to at least have them as experimental features by then.

You can find these under the Ideas column.

See you there

We won't be waiting to ship all of these improvements as one big release; instead, we will constantly be releasing as we merge them, so you will be hearing from us quite a bit as we go and will be able to benefit from them immediately. Once we complete all of them, we will declare Wasp 1.0.

If you have any additional ideas on what you would love to see in Wasp 1.0, let us know on our Discord or on GitHub!

That's it, the destination is locked in: next stop, Wasp 1.0! See you there!

articles.title: How I build products with AI: from a brainstorm to a production release
articles.description: When I start a product, I open ChatGPT before I open a coding agent.  I want to work through the idea...
articles.body_html:
When I start a product, I open ChatGPT before I open a coding agent.

I want to work through the idea before anything starts creating files. Who needs this product? What belongs in the first version? What am I deliberately leaving out? I want to settle those questions while changing my mind still means editing a document.

Then I move between tools: ChatGPT for the requirements, Antigravity for the GitHub backlog, Copilot CLI for implementation, and Claude Code for review. I read the final pull request myself before deciding whether to merge. GitHub Actions carries the work through validation and deployment, with different triggers for previews and production releases.

I also want the same engineering setup when I switch tools or start another product. I use skills for that, and I created dotcraft, my plugin of skills and agents for .NET, Blazor, and MudBlazor. It gives me a reusable starting point instead of another setup to assemble.

My setup:

Work Tool Model or setting
Brainstorming and PRD ChatGPT GPT-6.1 Sol, high reasoning
Initial application logo ChatGPT PRD as context
Everyday work without a model preference GitHub Copilot Copilot Fusion
Epics and child issues Antigravity with GitHub CLI Gemini 3.8 Flash, high reasoning
Epic implementation GitHub Copilot CLI with dotcraft GPT-6.1 Luna (or Copilot Fusion), Max reasoning, YOLO mode
AI review Claude Code app or CLI Claude Opus 5.5
UI work Copilot or Antigravity with the relevant skills A deliberate choice: GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, or Gemini Flash
Repeatable browser checks Playwright Automated user flows and assertions
Final review Me Read the code and check the behavior
Delivery and releases GitHub Actions CI, development previews, and production deployment

The model names will change. What I want to keep is the context: a decision made during the brainstorm needs to survive all the way to the code I merge.

Lately, Fusion is my default

I don't choose a model manually for every request. Lately, I use Copilot Fusion for most work where I don't already have a reason to pick a particular model. I give it the task and let it handle model selection.

Copilot Fusion selected at the Standard tier in my model picker.

UI work is an example of when I do have a preference: I might specifically want GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra. That is when I make the choice myself. For the rest, Fusion has been working very well for me, and I have found it helps keep my token costs down. I haven't measured a fixed saving per task.

I switched to Copilot Fusion recently because I was experimenting with it during the Preview (it was called HydraFusion) but I was not enthusiast about the outcomes.

I keep the model and billing details in my GitHub Copilot guide in the Resources section of my website. The named-model handoffs below describe particular parts of my workflow; Fusion is what I increasingly use between those cases.

The PRD carries my decisions between tools

My ChatGPT conversation ends with a product requirements document, or PRD, in the repository. I use GPT-6.1 Sol with high reasoning to work through the scope before asking for that document.

"Users can export their data" is the sort of requirement I want to question here. Which data? Which format? Does it include archived records? If I leave those decisions open, the implementation agent has to make them for me.

I put the PRD somewhere every tool can read it, such as docs/PRD.md. If I change a requirement, I update the file. A decision that exists only in my ChatGPT conversation is missing context for the next session.

The PRD also gives me a starting point for the initial application logo. I use it in ChatGPT to explain the product and audience, ask for a few directions, and choose one before generating the image. At this stage, I care about whether the logo works in an application header and as a small icon.

Sometimes I also use the logo-generator skill by op7418. That is a separate skill I use alongside dotcraft.

Then I open Antigravity and ask Gemini 3.8 Flash with high reasoning to turn the PRD into epics and child issues through the GitHub CLI. In my experience, this step has been accurate and inexpensive. I still check the backlog before implementation starts.

This is a reusable version of the request:

Read docs/PRD.md and the repository instructions.
Check existing issues and the applicable issue templates,
including account defaults.

Use the GitHub CLI to create epics and child issues.
Each epic needs a product outcome and scope.
Each child issue needs acceptance criteria, dependencies,
and a reference to the relevant PRD section.

Use native parent/sub-issue relationships.
Do not invent requirements or create duplicates.
Report unresolved decisions and return the created issue URLs.

I don't need to create and link every issue by hand. I do need to check that the agent has preserved the scope. A backlog full of clear titles can still describe a different product from the one I intended.

I check all the Epics and Issues anyway and I fix something if I see something that I don't really like so much.\
I like also this approach because if something that AI implement and I don't like it, I can always rework on the single task or epic using the same description and prompt.\
It helps to obtain always the same outcome.

dotcraft is how I keep my setup with me

For my .NET products, I want business logic to live in the application services and component tests to follow the same conventions. Switching from Copilot to Claude Code should not mean explaining those choices again.

That is why I created kasuken/dotcraft. It packages skills I have written, adapted, or curated from other projects, together with agents for implementation, review, and cleanup. I can maintain the shared guidance in one place and reuse it across products.

One shared setup for the .NET products I build. The repository also credits the skills' upstream sources.

For example, blazor-saas-stack describes my default architecture. bunit-testing provides guidance for component tests. dotnet-validate defines the verification expected before a change is called done. I don't want to paste all of those instructions into every implementation prompt.

The agents give the work separate roles: csharp-expert implements .NET changes, code-reviewer reads the result and reports findings, and janitor handles cleanup in small steps.

The implementation agent is instructed to validate its changes and hand them to the reviewer. Those instructions still need to be checked against what happened in the session.

In Copilot CLI, I install the plugin with:

copilot plugin marketplace add kasuken/dotcraft
copilot plugin install dotcraft@dotcraft

dotcraft also documents installation for Claude Code and Codex. Each client needs its own setup; installing a plugin in Copilot does not configure Antigravity. For Antigravity, I make the relevant skills available in a supported skill location.

The product's own instructions take precedence over dotcraft's defaults. I keep project decisions in AGENTS.md and the instruction files the client recognizes, then check that the client has found them. In Copilot CLI, /instructions and /skills list help me inspect the setup. A skill appearing in the list establishes availability; I still check that it is loaded when the task needs it.

I also maintain kasuken/.github for shared issue and pull request templates. The feature request form asks for the problem before the proposed solution. The PR checklist asks for testing evidence and includes a check that the app still works with billing disabled.
Using this approach, I don't need to configure common things in all my repos and I increase the bootstrapping of a new project.

The shared PR template gives me specific questions to ask of a change, including what happens when paid features are disabled.

GitHub supplies these supported defaults when a repository has no local equivalent. They are not copied into a clone, so a local agent may need to fetch them. I ask for that explicitly rather than assume a PR created through gh will contain the checklist.

DayPulse gave me a useful example

For DayPulse, one of my private projects, GPT-6 Sol produced the PRD and I gave it to Antigravity to create the backlog. The Today Screen epic had two child issues.

The first covered the localized date and the empty state when there was no check-in for the user's local day, with an action leading to /checkin. The second covered the completed check-in summary, including optional metrics, activities, notes, and navigation to edit or view the entry.

DayPulse's check-in screen with mood and energy selected. Screenshot from my application.

That local-day requirement is a detail I care about. "Show today's check-in" leaves room for an implementation to use the server's date. Specifying the user's local day gives me something concrete to check in the code and tests. The summary issue also explicitly required disabled metrics to stay hidden.

I handed GPT-6 Luna with Max reasoning the whole epic in one request. I then asked Claude Opus 5.5 to review the implementation across the epic; it reported no findings.

The issue completion notes recorded 253 passing tests after the first child issue and 284 in the final Release validation, with no build warnings or errors. Those are reported validation totals, including existing tests. They are not counts of tests the agent wrote for those two issues.

For me, the useful result was being able to compare the implementation with those specific acceptance criteria. A review with no findings doesn't answer whether I asked for the right product behavior.

I hand Copilot an epic with a clear stopping point

For the explicit-model implementation route described here, I open Copilot CLI with dotcraft installed, select GPT-6 Luna with Max reasoning, and enable YOLO mode. Some single-issue runs have used around 10–15 Copilot credits in my experience; that is a rough observation, not a price to budget against.

My request covers the epic and its child issues, with a separate commit for each issue and one pull request at the end:

Implement the epic at <EPIC_URL> and all its child issues.
Read the repository instructions, PRD, and applicable installed skills.
Work on a dedicated feature branch and respect issue dependencies.

Validate each child issue against its acceptance criteria.
Automate repeatable browser flows with Playwright where applicable.
Report automated coverage and anything that still needs a manual check.
Create a coherent commit for each issue and reference its URL.
Record completion and actual validation results on the issues.

Close the epic only when every child issue is implemented and validated.
Leave blocked work open and explain the blocker.

Create a PR using the applicable template, including an issue-to-commit
mapping, validation results, and remaining limitations.
Do not merge the PR.

One commit per issue lets me inspect the parts of the epic separately. In this workflow, closing the epic means implementation is ready for review; it does not mean the feature has shipped.

YOLO mode removes repeated approval prompts through Copilot's allow-all permissions. It does not make the commands safe. I am choosing to give the agent that permission, and I remain responsible for what it does.

After Copilot opens the PR, I ask Claude Code to review the implementation across the whole epic. I usually keep review fixes in that PR and rerun the affected checks if the code changes. I need validation for the version I am considering merging.

Then I read the final code myself and check the behavior against the requirements. That is where I decide whether to accept the work.

UI work gets a different route through the same process

For UI work, I want to choose the model myself when I have a particular result in mind. That might mean GPT-6.1 Sol or GPT-6 Astra in Copilot. I also use Antigravity with Gemini Flash, which has given me good UI results. I choose the tool and model for that piece of work, then return to Fusion when I have no reason to keep a specific model selected.

For the "general" UI and Design System I love the skill frontend-design because it helps AI to create the correct UI based on the context of the application and not the typical slop AI.

I bring in skills such as mudblazor-design-system, better-layout, and better-typography to make the request more specific. I also check keyboard and focus behavior. A screenshot helps me judge the layout, but I still need to use the form and see what happens in the empty state.

The requirements stay in the repository and the result still gets reviewed. Changing the tool for UI work should not mean losing the acceptance criteria I already settled.

I automate the repeatable browser checks with Playwright

I try to automate as much of the application testing as I can with Playwright. I don't want to click through the same screens manually after every change when a browser test can repeat the steps and check the result for me.

For a flow like DayPulse's check-in, I want the test to start from the empty Today screen, create an entry, verify the summary, edit the entry, and check that the updated values appear. Opening each page successfully isn't enough; the assertions need to cover the behavior in the acceptance criteria. This is the kind of repeatable journey I want automated as the product grows.

In Brainy, the CI workflow already has a separate Playwright end-to-end test job. It runs against the application with a real SQL Server database and is configured to upload traces and screenshots when tests fail. That gives me something to inspect when a browser test breaks, alongside the agent's explanation.

I still review whether the interface makes sense and explore behavior the tests don't cover. My aim is to spend that time on things that need my judgment, while Playwright handles the checks I would otherwise repeat by hand. I also review the tests: they need to fail when the expected behavior breaks.

I finish the backlog, then check the application as a whole

I repeat the implementation and review loop for the remaining epics in the release scope. Before calling that scope complete, I go back through the parent epics and their child issues. I want to see which PR contains the implementation, what was validated, and whether anything is still blocked or deliberately deferred.

An agent closing an epic is useful bookkeeping, but I still reconcile it with the merged code. If a child issue is incomplete, I leave it open. If I decide a feature belongs in a later release, I update the scope rather than close the issue as though it had been implemented.

I can ask an agent to help with that final pass:

Review the epics in the current release scope against the PRD,
their child issues, and the merged pull requests.

For each epic, report the implementation PRs, validation evidence,
and any unmet acceptance criteria. Check the child issues themselves;
do not rely only on the parent's checklist or closed status.

Close remaining issues only when the implementation and validation
support doing so. Leave blocked or deferred work open and explain why.
Report any requirements that are missing from the backlog.

Then I check the application across those epic boundaries, using automated browser tests for the repeatable journeys and manual checks for the remaining gaps. In DayPulse, the empty Today screen, the check-in form, and the completed summary need to work as one flow. Reviewing each screen separately would leave that journey unchecked.

The same applies to UI changes made late in the process: a better layout still needs to preserve navigation, validation, and the behavior described in the issues. I make corrections through the same issue and PR loop, so the fix gets reviewed too.

GitHub Actions gives me a development preview

I don't want deployment to depend on an agent remembering a sequence of terminal commands. I keep the build, test, and deployment steps in GitHub Actions so that the repository describes how the application gets published.

DayPulse is a concrete example. Its workflow runs a Release build and the test suite before the deployment job can start. For pull requests from the same repository, it is configured to publish the Blazor WebAssembly application to an Azure Static Web Apps preview environment. That gives me a development preview associated with the PR, before the change reaches production.

This is where I can check the published application in the browser. DayPulse is also a PWA, so I need to check installation, offline reload, and upgrades against a published build. The local development server alone doesn't cover those behaviors.

After I accept and merge the change, the push to main triggers DayPulse's build, test, and deployment workflow for production. Closing the PR also triggers cleanup of its preview environment. The automation handles the repeated publishing steps; I still check the workflow result and the deployed application.

Production releases have an explicit trigger

My server-hosted SaaS applications use a different production path. For Brainy, LearnStack, MoneyBrain, and Needly, I maintain a shared release workflow in kasuken/.github. Each application calls it from a small workflow in its own repository.

For these applications, merging to main runs CI without automatically deploying to production. I choose when to cut a release; GitHub Actions then handles the deployment. The distinction matters to me because several reviewed epics can belong to one release.

The release instructions let me choose a patch, minor, or major bump. For example, this starts a patch release for Brainy:

gh workflow run release.yml -R kasuken/Brainy -f bump=patch
gh run watch -R kasuken/Brainy

For that new-release path, the workflow resolves the next version, waits for passing CI on the commit being released, and builds a versioned application package. It deploys that package to Azure App Service through the GitHub production environment, using OIDC for Azure authentication.

Database changes are part of that delivery path too. Needly's migrations run before deployment; the other applications in this shared setup apply them on startup. I need to account for that difference when reviewing a release, especially if I might need to restore an earlier application version.

The workflow then checks the readiness endpoint, any configured extra pages, and the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect. On the workflow-dispatched new-release path, it creates the version tag and GitHub release only after deployment and those smoke checks succeed. It uses the matching changelog section for the notes when one exists, or generates notes from the merged PRs.

That is another part of the setup I want to maintain once. An improvement to the shared workflow can serve several products, while the application repositories supply their own project paths and deployment targets.

After deployment, I still have a product to check

A passing readiness check tells me the application responds. I also want evidence that the user flow I intended to release still works. I use automated checks where that behavior is covered and focus my manual review on the remaining gaps. For DayPulse, the Today and check-in journey, including the local-day behavior, remains the reference for what needs checking in the published application.

If I find a problem, it goes back into an issue with reproduction steps and the behavior I expected. I can give that bounded task to an agent, review the correction, and send it through the same delivery process. The backlog remains useful after the initial implementation.

For applications using my shared release workflow, I can redeploy an earlier version tag when I need to roll back. That restores the earlier application code; it does not reverse database migrations. I need to check that the older version still works with the current schema before choosing that route.

This is where the workflow reaches a release: the code has been reviewed, the intended version has been deployed, and I have checked the relevant behavior in the running application. Closing all the epics gets me to that final check; it doesn't replace it.

I like working this way in Omarchy

In Omarchy, I keep the browser full-screen on one workspace and three or four terminals tiled on another. Copilot can be working in one terminal while I inspect tests or Git history in another. Switching workspaces and moving focus with the keyboard lets me keep those layouts in place.

Four-way tiling, shown in the official Omarchy navigation manual. This is the manual's example desktop.

I have tried to reproduce the same behavior on Windows. Getting the tiling, workspace switching, and window focus to feel the way I want has taken more effort there. On Omarchy, I spend less time rearranging the desktop.

The searchable clipboard history is useful when I am carrying an issue URL or prompt between tools. I also like the themes running through the terminal and supported agent clients. I like sitting down at this machine, and that matters when it is where I build my products.

Searching copied text, from the official Omarchy clipboard manual. The example shows how a copied command can be found again.

I still spend attention on the scope, the backlog, and the final review. dotcraft saves me from rebuilding the engineering setup, and GitHub Actions handles the repeated release steps. Neither can decide whether DayPulse should show that metric or whether a feature belongs in the first release. Those decisions are still mine, and I want to see them reflected in the application I publish.

articles.title: Your Login Works. Now Prove Who Did What
articles.description: Keycloak audit logs help SaaS teams understand who did what, when an action happened, and which...
articles.body_html:
Keycloak audit logs help SaaS teams understand who did what, when an action happened, and which account or system performed it. Authentication tells you that someone successfully logged in. It doesn't automatically give you a complete record of what happened after that login.

Imagine a customer reports that an employee's account was removed, an administrator's permissions changed, or access to a sensitive resource was modified. Your application may confirm that the person had an active session, but can your team identify who made the change, when it happened, and whether it was intentional?

This is where audit logging becomes essential. As a SaaS product grows, more people gain access to administrative dashboards, customer data, configuration settings, and internal tools. Without a reliable audit trail, investigating an unexpected change can turn into a frustrating search across application logs, identity systems, and support conversations.

Keycloak provides useful event logging capabilities for authentication activity and administrative operations. Understanding what these events capture, how to configure them, and where their limitations lie helps SaaS teams build a clearer record of activity across their identity infrastructure.

TL;DR

Keycloak audit logs help SaaS teams track authentication activity and administrative changes, including who performed an action, what happened, and when it occurred. To build a useful audit trail, enable user and admin events, configure retention, and centralize logs for easier investigation.

Here are the key things to know:

  • User events: Track logins, logouts, failed authentication attempts, and credential changes.
  • Admin events: Identify administrative operations such as role assignments, user updates, and configuration changes.
  • Event details: Enable Include Representation to capture additional information about administrative requests.
  • Centralized logging: Send relevant events to a logging platform to investigate activity across your infrastructure.
  • Application-level auditing: Record business actions inside your SaaS because Keycloak doesn't capture every operation performed within your application.

With the right combination of identity events and application audit logs, your team can build a clearer history of activity and investigate security incidents with more confidence.

Authentication Events and Administrative Events: What's the Difference?

Keycloak audit logs cover two important types of activity: events generated by users during authentication and actions performed by administrators through the Keycloak Admin Console or Admin REST API.

Both matter when you're investigating a security issue, but they answer different questions.

User events: What happened during authentication?

User events record activity associated with authentication and account operations. Examples include:

  • Successful logins and logout events.
  • Failed login attempts caused by incorrect credentials.
  • Password updates and credential changes.
  • Account registration and profile updates.
  • Password reset and email verification attempts.

Keycloak provides different event types for these operations, and administrators can select which ones to save through the User events settings.

These records help your team investigate suspicious sign-in activity, repeated authentication failures, and changes to user credentials.

For example, if a customer reports that someone accessed their account without permission, your team can inspect the user's login history and look for unusual activity. A failed login followed by a successful login from an unfamiliar IP address may provide useful context for the investigation.

User events help establish what happened during authentication, including the event type, timestamp, and available user or client details.

Admin events: Who changed your identity configuration?

Administrative events record operations performed through Keycloak's administrative interfaces. They can help you identify who changed a configuration, which resource was affected, and what operation was performed.

Examples include:

  • Creating, updating, or deleting a user.
  • Assigning or removing roles.
  • Changing client configurations.
  • Updating realm settings.
  • Modifying groups and identity-related resources.

Consider a situation where a customer suddenly gains administrator permissions. A successful login event won't explain how that happened. An admin event can help your team trace the role assignment back to the administrative operation that changed the user's permissions.

Keycloak also provides an Include Representation option for admin events. When enabled, it records the JSON representation sent through the Admin REST API, giving administrators more detail about the changes made. This can increase database storage usage, so teams should account for the additional data when configuring event retention.

One important detail when investigating admin events is how Keycloak identifies the administrator who performed an operation. The event's authDetails field contains authentication details such as the realm, client, user ID (userId), and IP address. Keycloak records the administrator's user ID, not their name. To identify the person behind the change, your team needs to use that ID to find the corresponding account in the Keycloak Users section.

How to Enable Keycloak Audit Logs

Keycloak supports event logging out of the box, but successful user events and administrative actions are not automatically saved in the Admin Console. You need to enable the event types your team wants to record.

You can configure both from the realm's event settings.

Enable user events

To save authentication and account activity:

  1. Open the Keycloak Admin Console.
  2. Select Realm settings.
  3. Open the Events tab.
  4. Select User events settings.
  5. Turn Save events ON.
  6. Set the event expiration period.
  7. Use Add saved types to select the additional event types you want to store.
  8. Save your changes.

Once enabled, open the Events section and select User events to review recorded activity. You can also filter the events to investigate a specific user or event type.

Enable administrative events

To record changes made by administrators:

  1. Open Realm settings.
  2. Select Events.
  3. Open Admin events settings.
  4. Turn Save events ON.
  5. Enable Include Representation to store the JSON representation of administrative requests, providing additional details about the changes made.
  6. Save your changes.

You can then open Events → Admin events to inspect the recorded operations.

One detail deserves attention: enabling admin events records the operations, while enabling Include Representation adds the request representation for more detailed investigation. This additional information can increase database storage requirements, so set an appropriate retention policy and monitor storage usage.

What Should a Useful Audit Log Record?

Collecting events is a good starting point, but a long list of timestamps and event names won't help much when your team needs to investigate an incident. Useful audit records need enough context to explain what happened and connect the action to the person or system responsible.

For a SaaS application, an audit record should capture as many of these details as the event makes available:

  • Actor: The user, administrator, or service account responsible for the action.
  • Action: The operation performed, such as login, role assignment, account update, or deletion.
  • Target: The user, client, group, realm, or resource affected.
  • Timestamp: When the operation occurred, with a consistent timezone.
  • Result: Whether the operation succeeded or failed.
  • Source details: Available context such as the client, IP address, or request information.

For example, imagine an administrator changes a customer's role from viewer to admin. A useful record should help your team identify the administrator who made the change, the affected account, the operation, and its timestamp.

That context makes it possible to answer practical questions during an investigation: Was the change authorized? Did the administrator make it intentionally? Were other accounts modified around the same time?

Keycloak's user and admin events provide identity-related information, while the level of detail available depends on the event and its configuration. Your application can add the business context that identity logs cannot capture on their own.

Centralize Your Keycloak Audit Logs

Keeping audit events inside Keycloak is useful when an administrator needs to inspect a recent login or configuration change. However, as a SaaS product grows, your team may need to investigate activity across several systems at once.

For example, a security incident could involve a suspicious login, a change to a user's permissions, and an unusual request to your application. If each system stores its own records in a separate place, connecting those events takes time.

Centralized logging gives your team one place to collect and analyze this information.

Keycloak supports event listeners that process user and administrative events. Its built-in Logging Event Listener writes error events to the server log at the WARN level and other events at DEBUG. Since DEBUG messages aren't included in server logs by default, teams that need successful events in their logs must configure the appropriate logging levels. Custom event listeners can also forward event data to external systems, allowing teams to integrate Keycloak activity into their existing logging infrastructure.

A typical setup might look like this:

  1. Keycloak generates a user or administrative event.
  2. An event listener processes the event.
  3. The event reaches your centralized logging platform.
  4. Your team searches, filters, and correlates it with application and infrastructure logs.
  5. Alerts notify the appropriate people when defined security conditions occur.

Platforms such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, and Splunk can help teams search and analyze logs from multiple services. The right destination depends on your existing infrastructure and how your team handles security monitoring.

The main benefit is context. Your engineers can compare a Keycloak role change with application activity around the same timestamp, making it easier to reconstruct what happened during an incident.

Audit Log Retention, Access, and Security

An audit trail is useful only when the records remain available, trustworthy, and accessible to the right people. Logging everything without a retention or access policy can create its own security and operational problems.

Three areas deserve attention.

Set a clear retention period

Keycloak lets administrators configure how long saved event records remain available through the event expiration setting. Choose a retention period that supports your investigation needs and fits your storage capacity.

For longer retention, send relevant records to a centralized logging platform with its own retention policy. This also helps preserve historical activity when older events expire from Keycloak's event store.

Protect audit records from unauthorized changes

Audit logs can contain sensitive information about users, administrators, clients, and infrastructure. Access to these records should be restricted to people who need them for security investigations or operational work.

Your logging platform should also have appropriate access controls and safeguards against unauthorized deletion or modification. A record that an administrator can quietly alter or remove provides limited value during a security investigation.

Avoid collecting unnecessary sensitive data

More detail does not always mean a better audit trail. Enabling Include Representation for admin events can capture JSON request details, which may increase storage usage and expose information that needs careful handling.

Review the information your team collects, restrict access, and apply appropriate retention rules. Your goal is to preserve enough context to investigate activity without retaining unnecessary sensitive data.

Where Keycloak Audit Logs End and Application Auditing Begins

Keycloak can tell you about authentication and administrative operations within your identity infrastructure. However, it cannot automatically explain every action a user performs inside your SaaS product.

This distinction also matters during SaaS user offboarding, where teams need to track account deactivation, session termination, and permission removal through a reliable user deprovisioning process.

Imagine a customer support agent logs in successfully, opens a customer account, changes its billing details, and exports a report. Keycloak can record the authentication activity, but the business operations happen inside your application.

Your application needs its own audit trail for actions such as:

  • Creating, updating, or deleting customer records.
  • Changing subscription plans or billing details.
  • Exporting or downloading sensitive information.
  • Inviting users or changing their application permissions.
  • Updating organization settings.
  • Approving or rejecting important business operations.

These records should identify the authenticated user, the action, the affected resource, and the timestamp. For sensitive operations, recording the previous and updated values can also help explain exactly what changed.

This is where the two audit layers work together. Keycloak provides identity-related activity, while your application records business-level actions. Combining both gives your team a more complete picture of what happened across a customer account.

Managing Keycloak Audit Logging with Skycloak

Running Keycloak in production means keeping your identity infrastructure reliable while maintaining control over how users, administrators, and applications access your SaaS platform. Audit logging is an important part of that responsibility. Your team needs visibility into authentication activity, administrative changes, and the configuration decisions that affect access across your environment.

Skycloak provides managed Keycloak hosting for SaaS teams that want the flexibility and control of Keycloak without having to operate the underlying hosting infrastructure themselves.

Skycloak includes:

  • Unlimited users on all plans: There are no user-count restrictions as your SaaS grows.
  • Full Keycloak admin access: Your team retains access to Keycloak's administrative features and configuration settings.
  • Four hosting regions: Deploy in the US, EU, Canada, or Australia.
  • Realm exports: Export your realm configuration for backup, migration, or other operational needs.
  • 21-day free trial: Try Skycloak without a credit card.

Audit Logging Features by Plan

Skycloak's audit logging features depend on the selected plan:

  • User events: Included from the Launch plan onward.
  • Admin events: Included from the Business plan onward, with 30 days of retention on Business and 90 days on Enterprise.
  • SIEM integration: Available on Enterprise, allowing teams to send audit events to external platforms such as Splunk.

These plan differences allow SaaS teams to choose the level of audit visibility and event retention that fits their requirements. For a complete breakdown, visit Skycloak's audit logs feature page.

If you're looking for managed Keycloak hosting with the flexibility to manage your own identity configuration, explore Skycloak's hosting options.

You can also explore Skycloak's pricing plans to compare the available options and choose the setup that fits your SaaS requirements.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Keycloak have built-in audit logging?
Yes. Keycloak includes built-in event logging for user activity and administrative operations. User events cover activities such as logins, logouts, and credential changes, while admin events record operations performed through the Admin Console and Admin REST API. You can enable both from Realm settings → Events.

Are Keycloak audit logs enabled by default?
Keycloak does not automatically save all user and administrative events in its event store. Administrators need to enable Save events in the user event settings and Save events in the admin event settings. You can also configure which user event types to retain and how long to store them.

Can Keycloak show who changed a user's roles?
Yes. Keycloak records administrative operations such as role assignments and user updates through admin events. Enabling Include Representation adds the JSON representation of the administrative request, providing more detail about the operation. This helps administrators investigate permission changes and identify the account responsible for the action.

Can Keycloak send audit logs to an external monitoring platform?
Yes. Keycloak supports event listeners that can process user and administrative events. Its built-in logging listener can write event information to server logs, while custom event listeners can integrate with external logging and monitoring systems. This allows teams to bring identity activity into a centralized environment for searching, analysis, and alerting.

Skycloak also offers hosting regions in the US, EU, Canada, and Australia, supports realm exports, and includes a 21-day free trial without a credit card.

Final Thoughts

A successful login tells you that authentication worked. When something goes wrong, your team needs more context: who made the change, which account was affected, when the operation happened, and what actually changed.

Keycloak audit logs give SaaS teams a practical way to track authentication activity and administrative operations across their identity infrastructure. Enabling the right events, configuring retention, and centralizing relevant records can make security investigations much easier.

Your application also has a responsibility to record business-level activity. When identity events and application audit trails work together, your team gets a clearer view of what happens across customer accounts and administrative workflows.

As your SaaS grows, that visibility becomes an important part of maintaining accountability, investigating incidents, and protecting customer data.

articles.title: Your AI's code is "almost right". Here are 7 ways it fools you, and the 30-second check for each
articles.description: The worst AI code isn't the code that crashes. Code that crashes, you notice.  The worst one looks...
articles.body_html:
The worst AI code isn't the code that crashes. Code that crashes, you notice.

The worst one looks right, passes a quick glance, and the AI says "Done! ✅". Then it breaks in production two weeks later.

You're not alone in this. In Stack Overflow's 2025 developer survey, the most common complaint about AI tools was "AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite" (66% of developers). In the 2026 survey, nearly half said they trust AI output only when they can check it easily.

So here's my list of how "almost right" sneaks in, with a check for each that takes about 30 seconds. I use AI coding tools every day, and I keep running into every one of these.

1. "Fixed!" … but nothing was run

The AI edits the code, explains the fix nicely and stops. No test ran. Sometimes a test command did run, but it found 0 tests and still exited green.

30-second check: ask "Which command did you run, and what was the exit code?" Then look at the output for the number of tests that actually ran. 0 passed is not a pass.

2. The tests pass because the test changed

The fastest way to make a red test green is to change the test, not the code. Look out for:

  • it.skip( / xit( / @pytest.mark.skip
  • expect(total).toBe(90) quietly becoming expect(total).toBeDefined()
  • a snapshot "updated" to match the new (wrong) output

30-second check: git diff -- '*test*' '*spec*' before you accept anything. If a test file changed and you didn't ask for that, ask why.

3. A function or package that doesn't exist

It reads perfectly: import { parseSafe } from "zod/utils". That function is not there. Or it suggests npm install of a package with a very believable name. Attackers now register those made-up names on purpose, so that slip can turn into a real risk.

30-second check: open the real docs or the npm page. A brand-new package with a handful of downloads is a red flag.

4. Only the happy path works

The demo input works. An empty list, null, a timezone, a 0, a very long string or a double click doesn't.

30-second check: ask the AI, "Which 3 inputs would break this?" Then run those 3. It is surprisingly honest when you ask that directly.

5. Errors get swallowed

The code stops crashing because the crash is hidden:

try {
  return await getOrders(userId);
} catch {
  return [];   // the user just sees "no orders"
}

Nothing fails, nothing logs, and the bug becomes a support ticket.

30-second check: search the diff for catch, || [], ?? null and except: pass. Each one should log, rethrow or have a reason.

6. The right answer for the wrong version

The code is correct for a version you don't use: the Next.js pages router in an app-router project, an old React Router API, a removed config option. It compiles in the AI's head, not in your project.

30-second check: compare the imports with the versions in your package.json (or lock file), and paste your version into the prompt next time.

7. Security that "works"

The login works, so it looks done. But the JWT is decoded instead of verified, the secret is hard-coded, or an API route never checks who is calling it.

30-second check: for every new route, ask "Who is allowed to call this, and where is that checked?" Search the diff for strings that look like keys.

The habit that catches most of these

Before accepting any AI change, run one command:

git diff --stat

Did it touch files you never mentioned? Did test files change? Is the diff 10× bigger than the task? That one look catches half of this list.

Your turn 👇

Which one has bitten you most recently? And what's the 8th way that's missing from this list? I'll add the best ones (with credit) to a follow-up post.

Small note: I got tired of doing checks 1 and 2 by hand, so I built a free Claude Code plugin, proof-of-done, that does them automatically, and a free security-audit skill for number 7.

const users = [

articles.title: Google Sheets is my favourite free backend
articles.description: I made a small game for my daughter. It's called Počítadlo ("counter" in Czech), and it's a simple...
articles.body_html:
I made a small game for my daughter. It's called Počítadlo ("counter" in Czech), and it's a simple counting game that helps her learn the basics of math: adding and subtracting up to 20, ten questions, a timer and a trophy when she beats her record. It runs as a PWA on her iPad.

After a few days I wanted to know how she actually uses it. How often does she play, which levels, how long does it take her, where does she make mistakes? And I wanted it as an email to me and my wife every evening, because nobody is going to open a dashboard.

The obvious answer is a database, an API and some email service. For a kids' game that's way too much. So I used a Google Sheet and Apps Script. It costs nothing, there's no server, and it took one evening, most of which was me fighting Google's settings.

In this post, I'll walk you through:

  • how the app sends data to a Google Sheet
  • how the Sheet sends a daily email
  • the gotchas that cost me most of that evening

The idea

Every Google Sheet can have an Apps Script attached to it (Extensions → Apps Script). Apps Script is just JavaScript running on Google's servers, and it can do two things that matter here:

  1. Be deployed as a web app: you get a URL, and doPost(e) runs every time someone POSTs to it.
  2. Run functions on a schedule and send email with MailApp.

So the Sheet is the database, the script is the API, and Gmail is the email service. All free.

Receiving data

The script side is tiny. Parse the JSON, append rows:

function doPost(e) {
  const events = JSON.parse(e.postData.contents);
  const sheet = SpreadsheetApp.getActiveSpreadsheet().getSheetByName("events");
  const rows = events.map((ev) => [new Date(), new Date(ev.ts), ev.type, ev.level, ev.seconds, ev.mistakes]);
  sheet.getRange(sheet.getLastRow() + 1, 1, rows.length, rows[0].length).setValues(rows);
  return ContentService.createTextOutput("ok");
}

Then Deploy → New deployment → Web app, Execute as: Me, Who has access: Anyone. You get a URL ending with /exec.

In the app, I send events like "app opened", "level started", "level finished in 53 seconds with one mistake". The call looks like this:

await fetch(URL, {
  method: "POST",
  mode: "no-cors",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "text/plain" },
  body: JSON.stringify(events),
});

Two things here are important:

  • text/plain, not application/json. A JSON content type makes the browser send a CORS preflight, and Apps Script can't answer it. With text/plain there's no preflight, and you still JSON.parse it on the other side.
  • no-cors means you can't read the response. A resolved fetch only tells you the request reached Google. Not that the script worked. Keep that in mind, it bit me later.

The iPad is not always online, so events go to a queue in localStorage first and get sent when there's a connection. Nothing gets lost when she plays in the car.

Sending the email

The report is a normal function. It reads the rows, counts games, best and average times per level, and lists the wrong answers. Then:

MailApp.sendEmail({ to: EMAILS, name: "Počítadlo", subject, htmlBody: html });

The name matters more than you'd think. Without it the email comes "from you", Gmail files it under Sent, and you think it never arrived. Ask me how I know.

For the schedule, you create a trigger:

function setup() {
  ScriptApp.newTrigger("check").timeBased().everyMinutes(15).create();
}

check does nothing before 19:00. After that, it sends the report once and remembers the date in PropertiesService. Why not just a daily trigger at 19:00? Read on.

The gotchas

This is where my evening went.

The trigger doesn't exist until you run setup by hand. Obvious in hindsight. Pasting the code creates nothing. You have to pick setup in the function dropdown and press Run. My first evening email never came because there was no trigger at all.

"At 19:00" means "sometime between 19:00 and 20:00". Google runs time triggers at any minute inside the window. A 15-minute check that sends on its first run after 19:00 gets you within 15 minutes, and if one run fails, the next one catches up.

403 "access denied" with access set to Anyone. The web app returned Google Drive's "you need access" page to everyone, even though the settings were right. It went away after I ran a function in the editor and approved the permissions. The script had simply never been authorized.

"Sorry, unable to open the file at this time." That's Apps Script telling you that you're logged into more than one Google account. Use a private window with only the account that owns the Sheet.

New deployment vs. new version. Deploy → New deployment gives you a new URL. To update the code and keep the URL, go to Manage deployments → Edit → Version: New version. The scheduled functions always run the latest saved code, so changes to the email need only a save.

Make it tell you it's alive. Since no-cors hides everything, I added a doGet that lists the triggers and when the last report went out. Opening the URL in a browser shows me whether the schedule exists.

Your hosting will play your game. The same evening there were app opens with no games in them. It was Vercel, opening every new deploy in a headless browser to take a screenshot for the dashboard. Now everything not running as the installed app gets a web- prefix on its session ID, and the email skips those. I don't drop them, just mark them. If the detection is ever wrong on the iPad, I still have the data.

Limits

This is not a real backend and I wouldn't pretend it is.

  • The web app URL is in your JavaScript, so anyone can POST to it. Validate what comes in. Worst case for me is junk rows in a spreadsheet.
  • A free Gmail account can send 100 emails a day with MailApp. For one report a day, fine.
  • It's slow and has quotas. For a few hundred rows a day from one iPad, I'll never notice. For your startup, use a real database.

Was it worth it?

Yes. For something like this, it's perfect. The whole thing is one script file, a spreadsheet I can open on my phone, and an email at 19:00. I already know she gets stuck on 20 − 7, and that she beat her Level 1 record in her second game of the evening.

If you have a small personal project that needs to store a bit of data or send you a summary, try a Sheet before you spin up a server. The code is on GitHub in the tracking folder.

What's your favourite "free backend" hack? Drop a comment.

articles.title: Securing an Angular Firebase AI App with Email/Password Authentication (Part 3: Lightweight Home Screen, Lazy CDK Dialog, and Header Navigation)
articles.description: We now have AuthService for authentication and SignInModalComponent for users to enter their email...
articles.body_html:
We now have AuthService for authentication and SignInModalComponent for users to enter their email and password, and we need a lightweight home screen (HomeComponent) to connect them. When a user is unauthenticated, clicking the Sign In button on the home screen opens the CDK Sign-In modal. The user then enters their email and password to complete authentication and navigate to the /dashboard route.

In addition, HeaderComponent no longer displays only static text. It now renders a Home icon link on the left edge and a conditional Sign-Out button on the right edge.


Caption: The unauthenticated Home screen displaying the left-aligned Home icon in the header, the "Sign In" button in the hero card, and the feature metadata cards.

Architecture & Mental Model

HomeComponent and HeaderComponent share the AuthService.isAuthenticated computed signal to coordinate the UI across three states:

  • Unauthenticated /home: HeaderComponent displays only the left-aligned Home icon link (/home), and HomeComponent renders the Sign In button.
  • Lazy-loaded CDK Dialog (openSignInModal()): Clicking Sign In dynamically imports SignInModalComponent and Dialog (@angular/cdk/dialog) with Promise.all(), keeping the CDK dialog and Signal Forms out of the initial main.js bundle.
  • Authenticated /dashboard and /home: Once signed in, HeaderComponent reveals the right-aligned Sign-Out button. When an authenticated user returns to /home, HomeComponent checks isAuthenticated() and displays the Launch Studio link (/dashboard) instead of the Sign In button. 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Header["HeaderComponent (app-header)"]
        HOME_ICON["HomeIconComponent ([routerLink]='/home')"]
        AUTH_HDR{"isAuthenticated()?"}
        SIGNOUT_BTN["SignOutIconComponent (onSignOut -> /home)"]
        AUTH_HDR -- "true" --> SIGNOUT_BTN
    end

    subgraph Home["HomeComponent (/home)"]
        RESTORE["constructor: ensureAuth().catch(...)"]
        AUTH_HOME{"isAuthenticated()?"}
        SIGNIN_BTN["Button: Sign In (openSignInModal)"]
        LAUNCH_LINK["Link: Launch Studio ([routerLink]='/dashboard')"]
        RESTORE --> AUTH_HOME
        AUTH_HOME -- "false" --> SIGNIN_BTN
        AUTH_HOME -- "true" --> LAUNCH_LINK
    end

    subgraph LazyModal["Deferred Modal Chunk"]
        IMPORT["Promise.all([import(SignInModalComponent), import('@angular/cdk/dialog')])"]
        INJECT["runInInjectionContext(#injector, () => inject(Dialog).open(...))"]
        IMPORT --> INJECT
    end

    SIGNIN_BTN --> IMPORT
    INJECT -- "Auth Success" --> AUTH_HOME
    INJECT -- "Auth Success" --> AUTH_HDR

1. Updating HeaderComponent with Home Navigation and Conditional Sign-Out

In HeaderComponent, we add home navigation and a conditional Sign-Out button:

  • Component imports: Imports HomeIconComponent, RouterLink, and SignOutIconComponent in the imports array.
  • Home link: Displays <app-home-icon /> inside an <a> tag with [routerLink]="homeLink" (APP_LINKS.HOME, or /home) to navigate to the home screen on click.
  • Sign-Out button: Shows the <app-sign-out-icon /> button only when isAuthenticated() is true; clicking it calls onSignOut() to sign out, update isAuthenticated(), and return to /home. 
// src/app/shared/ui/layout/header/header.component.ts
@Component({
  selector: 'app-header',
  imports: [HomeIconComponent, RouterLink, SignOutIconComponent],
})
export class HeaderComponent {
  readonly homeLink = APP_LINKS.HOME;
  readonly #authService = inject(AuthService);
  readonly #router = inject(Router);
  readonly isAuthenticated = this.#authService.isAuthenticated;

  async onSignOut(): Promise<void> {
    await this.#authService.signOut();
    await this.#router.navigate([APP_LINKS.HOME]);
  }
}

<!-- src/app/shared/ui/layout/header/header.component.html -->
<header>
  <a [routerLink]="homeLink" aria-label="Go to Home Screen">
    <app-home-icon />
  </a>
  <h1>Firebase AI Logic Obscure Fact Speech Generator</h1>
  @if (isAuthenticated()) {
    <button type="button" (click)="onSignOut()" aria-label="Sign out">
      <app-sign-out-icon />
    </button>
  }
</header>

2. Building the Lightweight HomeComponent & Lazy-Loading the CDK Dialog

2.1 Restoring Auth State in the Constructor (ensureAuth().catch(...))

We need to ensure that the Firebase Auth Emulator and Firebase Auth are properly initialized when HomeComponent is constructed. However, a constructor() cannot be async, so we must execute this.#authService.ensureAuth() with a Promise chain instead of async/await.

The .catch() block logs and silently swallows any error without rethrowing it. Because this background task does not require the user's attention, showing an error message here would only cause confusion and unwanted panic.

// src/app/features/home/home.component.ts (Part 1: Fields & Constructor)
@Component({
  selector: 'app-home',
  imports: [RouterLink, ArrowRightIconComponent],
})
export class HomeComponent {
  readonly dashboard = APP_LINKS.DASHBOARD;
  readonly #authService = inject(AuthService);
  readonly isAuthenticated = this.#authService.isAuthenticated;
  readonly #injector = inject(Injector);
  #dialogRef: DialogRef<unknown, SignInModalComponent> | null = null;
  #isOpeningModal = false;

  constructor() {
    this.#authService.ensureAuth().catch((error) => console.error('Failed to restore auth session:', error));
  }

2.2 Lazy-Loading @angular/cdk/dialog & Solving the NG0203 Injection Context Error with runInInjectionContext

When opening the Sign-In modal in openSignInModal(), we keep the initial bundle small while preserving Angular's injection context:

  • Keeping main.js lightweight: Because HomeComponent is eagerly loaded into the main.js bundle, any static import increases its raw size and transfer time.
  • Lazy-loading @angular/cdk/dialog and the NG0203 error: We optimize the bundle by dynamically importing SignInModalComponent and @angular/cdk/dialog in openSignInModal(). However, calling inject(Dialog) after await Promise.all(...) throws an NG0203 error because it runs outside a valid injection context.
  • Restoring the injection context: We solve this by running the dialog logic inside the callback of runInInjectionContext using HomeComponent's Injector (this.#injector).
  • Why runInInjectionContext over a higher-order function: Using runInInjectionContext lets us assign this.#dialogRef = dialogRef directly inside an arrow function, which is cleaner than passing .bind(this) to a higher-order function.

2.3 Preventing Duplicate Modals & Resetting this.#dialogRef on Close (dialogRef.closed.subscribe)

In openSignInModal(), we prevent duplicate Sign-In modals and clean up the dialog reference on close:

  • Guarding against duplicate modals: #isOpeningModal and #dialogRef prevent opening multiple Sign-In modals; when either is truthy, a modal is already opening or open, so the method exits early.
  • Lazy-loading and opening the modal: Otherwise, we dynamically import SignInModalComponent and @angular/cdk/dialog with Promise.all(), inject Dialog to open the modal, and store its reference in this.#dialogRef.
  • Resetting #dialogRef on close: Subscribing to dialogRef.closed resets this.#dialogRef to null when the modal closes, allowing the dialog to be reopened later. 
// src/app/features/home/home.component.ts (Part 2: openSignInModal)
  async openSignInModal(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.#isOpeningModal || this.#dialogRef) {
      return;
    }

    this.#isOpeningModal = true;
    try {
      const [{ SignInModalComponent }, { Dialog }] = await Promise.all([
        import('@/shared/ui/sign-in-modal/sign-in-modal.component'),
        import('@angular/cdk/dialog'),
      ]);
      runInInjectionContext(this.#injector, () => {
        const dialog = inject(Dialog);
        const dialogRef = dialog.open(SignInModalComponent, {
          backdropClass: ['bg-surface-card'],
        });

        this.#dialogRef = dialogRef;
        dialogRef.closed.subscribe(() => (this.#dialogRef = null));
      });
    } finally {
      this.#isOpeningModal = false;
    }
  }
}

2.4 Conditional CTA Rendering in home.component.html

In home.component.html, the isAuthenticated() computed signal determines which button to display—including when a user navigates back to /home by typing /home in the address bar or clicking the Home icon in HeaderComponent:

  • When isAuthenticated() is true: The Home screen renders a Launch Studio link ([routerLink]="dashboard") that routes directly to /dashboard.
  • When isAuthenticated() is false: The Home screen renders a Sign In button ((click)="openSignInModal()") that opens the CDK Sign-In modal. 
<!-- src/app/features/home/home.component.html (CTA excerpt) -->
@if (isAuthenticated()) {
  <a [routerLink]="dashboard">
    <span>Launch Studio</span>
    <app-arrow-right-icon />
  </a>
} @else {
  <button type="button" (click)="openSignInModal()">
    <span>Sign In</span>
  </button>
}


Caption: The authenticated Home screen displaying the Home icon on the left and Sign-Out icon on the right of the header, and the "Launch Studio" button in the hero card.

Takeaways

In Part 3, we completed our authentication flow by connecting HomeComponent, SignInModalComponent, and HeaderComponent:

  • Conditional Actions in HomeComponent: We built a lightweight HomeComponent that conditionally renders the Sign In and Launch Studio buttons based on the isAuthenticated() signal. When isAuthenticated() is false, it displays the Sign In button; when true, it displays Launch Studio.
  • Lazy CDK Sign-In Modal Flow: Clicking Sign In opens the CDK SignInModalComponent where users enter their email and password. When the credentials are valid, the modal navigates the user to the /dashboard route; otherwise, it displays an authentication error message.
  • Resolving NG0203 with runInInjectionContext: Injecting Dialog after await Promise.all(...) in openSignInModal() triggers Angular's NG0203 error because the async continuation runs outside an injection context. We resolve this by executing the dialog logic inside the callback of runInInjectionContext using HomeComponent's Injector.
  • Header Navigation and Sign-Out: HeaderComponent adds home navigation and sign-out functionality. It always displays the Home icon to navigate back to the /home screen when clicked, while the conditional Sign-Out icon allows authenticated users to sign out from Firebase Auth and reset the isAuthenticated() signal to false.
