  • Angular Dependency Injection Context (runInInjectionContext)

articles.title: Svelte 5 Isn't Pure Compiler Magic: How Runes, Fine-Grained Signals, and Direct DOM Mutations Actually Work Under the Hood
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into Svelte 5 internals. Learn why Svelte shifted from compile-time dirty checking to runtime signals, how the Push-Pull reactive dependency graph works, how the compiler compiles templates into direct DOM operations without a Virtual DOM, and when to use $state.raw for maximum performance.
articles.body_html:
When Svelte first captured the web development community, it arrived with a bold manifesto:

"Virtual DOM is pure overhead. Svelte runs at build time, converting your components into tiny, highly efficient vanilla JavaScript that surgically updates the DOM."

For five years, developers celebrated Svelte's compile-time reactivity. You did not need useState, dependency arrays, or reconciliation engines. You simply wrote ordinary JavaScript:

<script>
  let count = 0;

  function increment() {
    count += 1;
  }
</script>

<button on:click={increment}>
  Clicks: {count}
</button>

Under the hood, Svelte 3 and 4 parsed your script, spotted the assignment operator (count += 1), and injected a hidden compiler helper called $$invalidate:

function increment() {
  $$invalidate(0, count += 1);
}

Whenever $$invalidate fired, Svelte flagged a bitmask dirty array on the component instance. On the next microtask, it walked through a switch statement in the generated update function and mutated the exact DOM node.

It felt like sorcery. But as applications scaled, that pure compile-time illusion began showing deep architectural cracks.

Reactivity only worked inside .svelte single file components. If you moved business logic into a standalone JavaScript file, the compiler could no longer rewrite your variable assignments. You had to abandon normal variables and reach for custom Svelte stores with manual subscriptions, readable contracts, and awkward boilerplate. Furthermore, tracking deep object mutations required reassigning the root object (user.profile.age = 30; user = user;), causing the entire component to re-evaluate its dirty checks.

With Svelte 5, the core team made an audacious architectural pivot. They walked away from pure compile-time assignment rewriting and adopted Runes: explicit primitives powered by a fine-grained, push-pull runtime signal graph.

Many developers were startled. Was Svelte turning into Solid or Vue? Did Svelte abandon its core philosophy?

The reality is far more fascinating. Svelte 5 did not surrender its compiler advantage; it elevated it. By combining static template hoisting with runtime signals, Svelte 5 achieves fine-grained reactivity without the clunky stores of Svelte 4, and without the Virtual DOM overhead of React.

Here is the mechanical breakdown of how Svelte 5 actually executes beneath your keyboard.

1. The Architectural Shift: Svelte 4 vs Svelte 5

To understand why Runes exist, you must inspect the assembly line of Svelte 4.

In Svelte 4, the compiler treated the entire .svelte component as the atomic boundary of reactivity. When you modified a variable, the component did not know which specific DOM node depended on which specific sub-property. The compiler only knew that something inside the component was dirty.

Here is what Svelte 4 generated for a simple counter:

// Svelte 4 Compiler Output (Conceptual)
function p(ctx, [dirty]) {
  // If bit 0 in the dirty bitmask is set:
  if (dirty & /*count*/ 1) {
    set_data(t1, /*count*/ ctx[0]);
  }
}

This model came with three severe limitations:

  1. The Component Boundary Trap: If you wanted reactive state shared across five components or held in a TypeScript utility file, you could not use let count = 0. You had to import writable(0) from svelte/store, wrap updates in count.update(n => n + 1), and use the special auto-subscription syntax ($count) inside templates.
  2. Coarse-Grained Dirty Checking: Every state change marked the entire component dirty. Even if only one text node changed, Svelte had to execute the component's p() update function, checking every active bitmask condition.
  3. Array and Object Mutation Pitfalls: Methods like array.push(item) did not trigger reactivity because no assignment operator existed for the AST parser to rewrite. Developers had to write array = [...array, item] purely to appease the compiler.

Svelte 5 solves this by moving reactivity from compile-time AST variable instrumentation to universal runtime signal nodes.

Instead of rewriting count += 1, Svelte 5 provides primitives called Runes ($state, $derived, $effect). These functions do not belong to a preprocessor; they are parsed into universal signal nodes that work identically inside .svelte files and universal .svelte.js or .svelte.ts modules.

2. Under the Hood of Runes: The Push-Pull Signal Graph

When you declare state in Svelte 5:

let count = $state(0);
let double = $derived(count * 2);

You are not creating a simple number. You are registering nodes inside a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of reactive dependencies.

A signal graph consists of three primary node types:

  • Source Nodes ($state): Hold raw values. When written to, they notify their dependents.
  • Computation Nodes ($derived): Depend on one or more sources or other computations. They recalculate only when their upstream dependencies change.
  • Consumer Nodes ($effect): Side effects and DOM update bindings that subscribe to sources or derivations and run when their inputs change.

Most naive signal implementations use an eager push mechanism: when a source changes, it immediately pushes the new value down every branch of the tree. This approach frequently causes the Diamond Problem, where a node that depends on two derived values is evaluated twice in intermediate, inconsistent states (a glitch).

Svelte 5 avoids this completely using a Push-Pull (or Mark-and-Sweep) algorithm.

The Push Phase (Marking Dirty)

When you write count++, Svelte does not immediately recalculate double or update the DOM. Instead, it enters a synchronous push phase:

  1. The $state(count) source node marks itself as dirty.
  2. It walks down its dependency links to $derived(double).
  3. It does not recompute double; it simply marks double with a status flag: DIRTY.
  4. It continues downstream to any active $effect connected to double, scheduling the effect into the microtask execution queue.

No application logic runs during the push phase. Only lightweight status flags are toggled.

The Pull Phase (Lazy Evaluation)

When the browser reaches the scheduled microtask or when application code reads double:

  1. The consumer pulls the value from $derived(double).
  2. The derivation checks its flag. If it is DIRTY, it checks its upstream dependency (count).
  3. It computes the new value (count * 2), caches the result, and clears its DIRTY flag.
  4. If double is read ten times without count changing, it returns the cached value in $O(1)$ time with zero recalculation.

This separation guarantees glitch-free execution. If two different derivations depend on the same counter and feed into a single effect, the effect runs exactly once, reading both values after all dirty marks have resolved.

3. The Compiler Pipeline: Turning Templates into Vanilla JS

If Svelte 5 uses runtime signals, what role does the compiler play?

This is where Svelte 5 departs dramatically from signal-based frameworks like SolidJS. SolidJS creates individual reactive wrappers around almost every element. Svelte 5 uses its compiler to perform Static Template Hoisting and Surgical Dynamic Attachment.

Consider this Svelte 5 component:

<script>
  let count = $state(0);
  let user = $state("Ada");
</script>

<div class="card">
  <h1>Welcome, {user}!</h1>
  <p>Static description text that never changes.</p>
  <button onclick={() => count++}>
    Clicks: {count}
  </button>
</div>

When you pass this file through svelte/compiler, the compilation passes through four distinct phases:

Phase 1: Parsing and AST Construction

The compiler parses the file into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), separating the <script> block, CSS styles, and HTML elements into structured nodes.

Phase 2: Static Analysis

The compiler walks the template tree and identifies which parts of the markup are completely static. In our example:

  • <div class="card"> is static.
  • <h1>Welcome, </h1> has static tags with one dynamic text slot ({user}).
  • <p>Static description...</p> is completely static.
  • <button> has a dynamic event listener and one dynamic text slot ({count}).

Phase 3: Template Hoisting ($.template)

Instead of compiling each HTML element into separate JavaScript document creation calls (document.createElement('div')), the compiler stringifies the entire invariant HTML structure into a single static string template:

// Compiled output (conceptual representation)
const root_template = $.template(
  `<div class="card">
    <h1>Welcome, <!>!</h1>
    <p>Static description text that never changes.</p>
    <button>Clicks: <!></button>
  </div>`
);

Notice the <!> comment markers. These serve as hydration anchors and insertion slots for dynamic expressions.

At application initialization, the browser calls document.createElement('template') and parses this HTML string natively in C++ through the browser engine. When a component instance mounts, Svelte clones this entire pre-parsed subtree using root_template(), which executes a single, hyper-fast document.importNode() clone.

Phase 4: Targeted Effect Subscriptions ($.render_effect)

Next, the compiler generates code that traverses directly to the dynamic slots without inspecting the static nodes:

export default function Component($$anchor) {
  let count = $.source(0);
  let user = $.source("Ada");

  const fragment = root_template();
  const div = $.first_child(fragment);
  const h1 = $.first_child(div);
  const user_text_slot = $.child(h1, 1);
  const button = $.sibling($.sibling(h1, 2), 2);
  const count_text_slot = $.child(button, 1);

  // Bind event listener
  button.__click = () => $.set(count, $.get(count) + 1);

  // Subscribe dynamic text nodes to signals
  $.render_effect(() => {
    $.set_text(user_text_slot, $.get(user));
  });

  $.render_effect(() => {
    $.set_text(count_text_slot, $.get(count));
  });

  $.append($$anchor, fragment);
}

Look closely at what happened.

The static <p> tag is never stored in a variable, never inspected by a reconciliation algorithm, and never diffed.

When count changes, only the second $.render_effect wakes up. It reads the new value and executes count_text_slot.data = new_value. The parent component function does not re-run. No intermediate JavaScript objects are allocated. The update is a direct, surgical $O(1)$ memory write.

4. Virtual DOM vs Direct Signal Mutation: The Real Memory Cost

To truly appreciate this architecture, compare it to how React handles the same counter button.

In React, state belongs to the component fiber. When you call setCount(count + 1):

  1. React marks the entire component fiber dirty.
  2. The scheduler re-executes the component function from top to bottom.
  3. Every JSX expression executes, instantiating fresh Virtual DOM JavaScript objects for the <div>, the <h1>, the <p>, and the <button>.
  4. The reconciler diffs the newly created virtual tree against the previous virtual tree.
  5. It discovers that the text node inside <button> changed, creates a DOM patch, and writes to the real DOM.
  6. The entire abandoned virtual tree is discarded and awaits garbage collection.

In simple apps, this process happens in a fraction of a millisecond. But in large dashboards, data tables, or heavy data-visualization tools with thousands of nodes, allocating and diffing virtual trees generates non-trivial CPU work and persistent garbage collection pressure.

In Svelte 5:

  • The component function runs once at mount.
  • When count increments, zero virtual DOM nodes are instantiated.
  • Zero diffing algorithms run.
  • The signal triggers its subscriber directly: node.data = count.

Because Svelte does not need a runtime reconciliation engine, the core client runtime weighs only a few kilobytes.

5. Deep Proxy Reactivity vs $state.raw: Performance at Scale

One of the most powerful features of Svelte 5 is deep object reactivity. In Svelte 4, mutating an array or nested object required reassignment gymnastics. In Svelte 5, $state wraps objects in JavaScript Proxy instances:

let settings = $state({
  theme: "dark",
  user: {
    notifications: {
      email: true
    }
  }
});

// Works seamlessly:
settings.user.notifications.email = false;

When you pass an object or array to $state(), Svelte recursively intercepts read and write operations. When you mutate settings.user.notifications.email, the proxy trap catches the write, identifies the exact signal node associated with that property path, and notifies only the effects reading that specific leaf property.

However, deep proxying comes with an engineering tradeoff: memory overhead.

If you fetch a dataset of 50,000 GeoJSON points, financial transactions, or WebGL coordinate buffers and wrap it in $state(), Svelte will recursively proxy every single object and array index in that collection. That proxy creation consumes significant CPU time and multiplies heap memory consumption.

To solve this, Svelte 5 introduced $state.raw.

When to Use $state.raw

$state.raw creates a shallow signal that does not proxy its contents:

// Creates a shallow signal with ZERO proxy wrapping
let bigData = $state.raw(largePayloadFromApi);

// This will NOT trigger reactivity:
bigData[0].selected = true;

// Reassigning the root reference DOES trigger reactivity:
bigData = bigData.map(item => 
  item.id === targetId ? { ...item, selected: true } : item
);

Use $state.raw whenever:

  1. You are managing large, immutable datasets (tables with thousands of rows, API responses).
  2. You are integrating third-party libraries that hold their own complex class instances (Three.js meshes, Leaflet map objects, Monaco editor instances). Wrapping these in Proxies can break internal identity checks (this === target).
  3. You only care about updates when replacing the entire reference.

By distinguishing between $state for interactive UI state and $state.raw for large data buffers, you can maintain optimal frame rates and minimal heap footprints.

6. Production Pitfalls: The $effect Trap

Because $effect resembles React's useEffect, developers transitioning to Svelte 5 often carry over dangerous habits.

The most common antipattern is using $effect for state synchronization:

// ❌ ANTIPATTERN: Redundant state synchronization
let count = $state(0);
let double = $state(0);

$effect(() => {
  double = count * 2;
});

Why is this dangerous?

  1. It forces two distinct render cycles. First, count changes and renders. Next, the effect runs, mutates double, and triggers a second render pass.
  2. It breaks the signal graph's push-pull guarantees, creating potential infinite loops if dependencies are not strictly isolated.

The idiomatic Svelte 5 approach is to use $derived:

// ✅ IDIOMATIC: Synchronous, lazy derivation
let count = $state(0);
let double = $derived(count * 2);

$derived calculates its value synchronously during the pull phase, costs zero effect scheduler overhead, and guarantees that downstream consumers always see consistent data on the very first render pass.

Reserve $effect strictly for true external side effects:

  • Manual DOM manipulation (canvas painting, focusing an input).
  • Setting up external event listeners or WebSocket subscriptions.
  • Logging analytics or saving state to localStorage.

7. Universal Reactivity in .svelte.js Modules

Perhaps the most transformative benefit of Svelte 5 is that reactivity is no longer trapped inside component markup.

In Svelte 4, building a reusable reactive state machine across files required custom stores:

// Svelte 4: Store boilerplate in cart.js
import { writable, derived } from 'svelte/store';

export const items = writable([]);
export const total = derived(items, $items => 
  $items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0)
);

export function addItem(item) {
  items.update(list => [...list, item]);
}

In Svelte 5, you create a standard .svelte.js or .svelte.ts file and write ordinary JavaScript classes or factory functions using Runes:

// Svelte 5: cart.svelte.ts
export class Cart {
  items = $state<Item[]>([]);
  total = $derived(this.items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price, 0));

  add(item: Item) {
    this.items.push(item);
  }

  remove(id: string) {
    this.items = this.items.filter(i => i.id !== id);
  }
}

export const cart = new Cart();

Any component that imports cart can read cart.total or call cart.add(item) directly. Because Cart uses native signals, components automatically subscribe to only the properties they access. If a component only reads cart.total, it will not re-evaluate when an individual item's thumbnail updates.

Reactivity is now a native language feature of your application architecture rather than a special syntax reserved for template files.

The Mental Shift

The transition from Svelte 4 to Svelte 5 is not an admission that compilers failed. It is the realization that the compiler and the runtime signal graph are strongest when working in harmony.

The compiler excels at static analysis: finding invariant HTML, hoisting templates into pre-parsed DOM clones, and isolating reactive holes at build time.

Runtime signals excel at dynamic dependencies: tracking relationships across module boundaries, managing deep object mutations without reassignment hacks, and executing push-pull updates without dirty bitmask arrays.

By pairing a specialized build-time compiler with a fine-grained signal engine, Svelte 5 delivers what front-end architectures have promised for a decade: the expressive simplicity of vanilla JavaScript variables with the surgical precision of direct DOM updates.

If you have migrated existing production applications to Svelte 5, how has the transition from Svelte 4 stores to Runes shaped your state architecture? Have you encountered cases where $state.raw made a measurable difference in memory consumption? Share your findings and architectural patterns in the comments below.

articles.title: getCurrentPosition() Has No Default Timeout. That's the Trap.
articles.description: A "find my location" button that works instantly on your laptop and hangs forever on a phone with a weak signal isn't flaky — it's getCurrentPosition() doing exactly what its defaults tell it to do. No timeout, no cached position, and a watcher nobody told to stop.
articles.body_html:
The ticket read: "location button sometimes just spins forever." Not a crash, not an error toast — just a spinner that never stopped. QA couldn't reproduce it. It worked every time on the office Wi-Fi, every time on a laptop, every time in the demo to the client.

It only happened out in the field. On a phone. Somewhere the GPS fix took its time and the Wi-Fi-based positioning fallback was slow to answer. Which meant it was exactly the one environment nobody tested in before shipping.

Here's the part that made it worse: the code had an error handler. Both arguments to getCurrentPosition() were filled in, success and failure. By every code-review instinct, this was handled.

The code that looks fully handled 

function useMyLocation(onFound, onFail) {
  navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(
    (pos) => onFound(pos.coords),
    (err) => onFail(err.message)
  );
}

A success callback, an error callback, nothing swallowed. If you squint, it even looks defensive — most getCurrentPosition() snippets you'll find in the wild look exactly like this.

Before you keep reading: what has to happen for that error callback to fire at all? Not "what does it do" — when does the browser decide to call it?

The honest answer is: only when the browser gives up and reports a GeolocationPositionError — permission denied, position unavailable, or a timeout. And a timeout is an option you pass in. If you don't pass one, there's nothing to time out. The browser just... keeps trying. Forever, if it has to. Neither callback is under any obligation to ever run.

The default timeout is not "some reasonable number." It's Infinity.

getCurrentPosition() takes a third, optional options argument: { enableHighAccuracy, timeout, maximumAge }. Skip it — like the snippet above does — and you get the spec's own defaults:

{ enableHighAccuracy: false, timeout: Infinity, maximumAge: 0 }

timeout: Infinity means precisely what it says: the call will wait as long as the device needs to produce a position, with no upper bound. On a laptop with recent Wi-Fi positioning data cached nearby, that's near-instant, so the bug never shows up in testing. On a phone with a weak signal indoors, "as long as it needs" can be minutes — or, if the underlying location provider never calls back at all, forever. There's no silent fallback, no eventual error. The spinner you built to show while waiting just keeps being accurate.

The other default nobody reads: maximumAge: 0

maximumAge controls whether the browser is allowed to hand back a cached position instead of asking the device for a brand-new fix. The default is 0 milliseconds — meaning no cache is old enough to use, ever. Every single call to getCurrentPosition(), even one fired a hundred milliseconds after the last one, forces a fresh GPS/Wi-Fi/cell fix from scratch.

That's rarely what you actually want. A "locate me" button a user double-clicks, or a component that calls getCurrentPosition() on mount right after a sibling component just did the same thing, don't need two independent fixes a tenth of a second apart. Passing a real maximumAge — "a position up to 30 seconds old is fine" — turns repeat calls into near-free cache hits instead of two full location requests:

navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(onFound, onFail, {
  timeout: 10_000,
  maximumAge: 30_000,
});

watchPosition() has the same shape of bug as a forgotten clearInterval

getCurrentPosition() asks once. watchPosition() asks continuously, calling your success callback every time the device's position changes meaningfully — useful for live tracking, useless the moment nobody's watching the screen anymore. It returns a watch ID, and that ID is your responsibility:

const watchId = navigator.geolocation.watchPosition(onMove, onError, {
  enableHighAccuracy: true,
});

// later, when you're done:
navigator.geolocation.clearWatch(watchId);

Skip that last line — the same way it's easy to skip clearInterval() — and the watch keeps running after the component that started it is gone. In a React component, that's a watchPosition() call in a useEffect with no cleanup function: the GPS radio stays active, the callback keeps firing into a component that no longer exists, and the battery drain shows up in a support ticket that has nothing to do with location on its face.

useEffect(() => {
  const id = navigator.geolocation.watchPosition(onMove, onError);
  return () => navigator.geolocation.clearWatch(id);
}, []);

One line in the cleanup function. Easy to write, easy to forget, and nothing in the API warns you that you forgot it.

It's not a Promise, and that's the last gotcha

getCurrentPosition() predates fetch(), predates Promise, and was never updated to support either — it's success/error callbacks, full stop. You can't await it directly. The fix is a wrapper you write once and reuse everywhere:

function getPosition(options) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(resolve, reject, {
      enableHighAccuracy: false,
      timeout: 10_000,
      maximumAge: 30_000,
      ...options,
    });
  });
}

try {
  const pos = await getPosition();
  useLocation(pos.coords);
} catch (err) {
  if (err.code === err.PERMISSION_DENIED) showPermissionHelp();
  else if (err.code === err.TIMEOUT) showRetry();
  else showGenericError();
}

Every default that bit the original snippet is now an explicit choice, and the whole thing reads top to bottom instead of nesting two callbacks inside each other.

The one real constraint: it needs a secure origin

This part isn't a trap, just worth stating plainly: every major browser requires a secure context — HTTPS, or localhost in development — before it will even ask for location permission. That's been true for close to a decade now, not a new restriction, and there's no workaround or flag to reach for; if a getCurrentPosition() call is silently failing in a way none of the above explains, check the protocol in the address bar first.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The playground above simulates the GPS fix with a slider, so you get the exact same race every time instead of waiting on whatever signal your actual device has right now. Set a slow "fix," turn on "use the default options," and watch the stopwatch climb with nothing to stop it — that's timeout: Infinity, reproduced on demand. Then try the watchPosition() panel: start it, hit "simulate component unmount" without stopping it first, and watch the counter keep climbing anyway.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The fix for that "spins forever" ticket was three lines: a timeout, a maximumAge, and a clearWatch() in a cleanup function that had never been written. None of it was hard once someone knew to look for it — the hard part was realizing that "sometimes it just hangs" wasn't a flaky bug report. It was the spec's own default, read literally.

Does your codebase have a bare getCurrentPosition() call anywhere without a timeout? Worth a five-minute grep before it becomes someone else's "impossible to reproduce" ticket.

articles.title: Don't Stop Believing in Foundational Knowledge 🙏🏼
articles.description: Fayaz argues why fundamental human knowledge is important, no matter how advanced AI becomes.
articles.body_html:
Imagine Artificial Super-intelligence (ASI) is achieved, and after the technology causes widespread socioeconomic turmoil, humanity decides that ASI will be free to all, but with some guardrails, regulations, and a reasonable token limit.

Imagine that, in that not-so-distant future society, you are one of the few who still have foundational knowledge of technology, programming, and software engineering.

Now, imagine yourself up against someone who is not good with computers or technology in general. Say that person's name is John.

In that scenario:

  1. Who will be able to create better and more reliable (to a human) software using ASI? John, or you?
  2. Who will have a better chance of saving humanity if ASI goes rogue? John, or you?

Some say that people who are trying to avoid facing the inevitable reality of highly capable AI are in denial. I agree. We were all there to some extent not so long ago.

On the other hand, people who are overhyping the use of AI in serious software development, without restrictions or proper human vetting, are being dangerously irresponsible.

Foundational human knowledge is essential for a better future. And that is especially true for the survival of our species against all sorts of future dangers.

Hence, we must strive to create a safe environment where learning and using foundational knowledge is highly valued. This will ensure that we retain our current knowledge and skills, and that future generations have enough incentive to do the same.

"Oh, look what I can produce with my little AI token count!" is not cute anymore.

We need to put government regulations in place to make sure AI-generated software is properly verified by humans through an actual, verifiable review process before it can be used in critical sectors such as government institutions, hospitals, banks, and schools. A skim-through session in the name of review is not enough.

Private and personal use can't be restricted anyway, but AI use in software development for the public sector must be regulated and monitored, with proper accountability attached to the review and release process.

That's essential to ensure that, one fine morning, we won't find ourselves in an unforeseeable AI apocalypse.

The solution to such a probable apocalypse is not more AI development; rather, the solution is in our responsible actions and in our very own foundational knowledge.

articles.title: Part 4: The Alert That Could Never Fire
articles.description: Since the first week of this project, observability/prometheus/alerts.yml has contained this:    -...
articles.body_html:
Since the first week of this project, observability/prometheus/alerts.yml has contained this:

- alert: PDSCircuitOpen
  expr: pybreaker_state{name="pds"} == 1

It is a correct rule. The circuit breaker in front of the Personal Demographics Service opens after five consecutive failures, the pipeline carries on with the demographics from the message, and somebody should be told.

No service has ever exported pybreaker_state. The rule has been watching a series that does not exist, which looks exactly like a healthy system.

The problem

Monitoring has a particular failure mode: you cannot tell the difference between nothing being wrong and nothing being watched. A dashboard with no red on it means one of those two things, and it does not say which.

In this pipeline, that matters more than usual, because the failures I care about mostly return 200. A patient written without an NHS number to match on is a successful request. A date of birth that failed to parse is a successful request. The breaker opening and the pipeline silently dropping to unenriched demographics is a whole shift of successful requests.

So this week I went looking for the things the pipeline does that nobody would ever find out about.

What the pipeline could not see

The breaker opens, and nothing says so

I started the transform service, sent a message, and scraped /metrics. Twenty-eight metric families, and pybreaker_state is not among them. Nothing with breaker or circuit in the name at all.

Then I drove the breaker open, which takes five failures:

breaker before      : closed | failures: 0
breaker after       : open   | failures: 5
pybreaker_state now : False

The breaker is open. The pipeline has stopped enriching. The alert cannot fire, and there is no other signal anywhere.

pybreaker makes this easy to fix. It has a CircuitBreakerListener with a state_change hook, which is called on every transition, so there is nothing to poll:

class _BreakerStateExporter(pybreaker.CircuitBreakerListener):
    def state_change(self, cb, old_state, new_state) -> None:
        BREAKER_STATE.labels(name=cb.name).set(
            _BREAKER_STATE_VALUES.get(getattr(new_state, "name", None), 0)
        )

That getattr(new_state, "name", None) is the second version. My first read new_state.state, which does not exist in pybreaker 1.2.0. The state objects carry a name instead, holding the string closed, open or half-open.

The failure mode of getting that wrong is the thing this whole article is about. getattr with a default does not raise. The lookup misses, falls back to 0, and the gauge sits there reading closed while the breaker is open. I would have shipped a fix for an unfireable alert that left it unfireable, and the metric would have existed, which is worse, because now the dashboard has a panel on it.

The test caught it.

Fields that fail to map leave no trace

Part 3 was about nine mapping defects. The reason all nine survived is in this article: only a whole-message parse failure goes to the dead-letter folder. A single field that fails to map is simply absent from the resource, and the message returns 200.

I sent a message with an unparseable date of birth:

message with an unparseable date of birth -> HTTP 200
birthDate in the resource : False
hl7_dlq_total moved?      : no
any metric for a lost field: none

The mapper now reports what it dropped, and transform turns that into
hl7_field_dropped_total{segment,field,reason}. The mapper itself stays free of Prometheus imports: it reports, the service counts. Known gaps like PID-11 and PV1-19 come through as not_mapped, so they are visible without being alarming, and unparseable_date is the one with an alert on it.

Alert rules are code that only runs during an incident

Which is the actual reason this sat here for weeks. Nothing in the build ever executed that rule.

Prometheus ships a unit test framework for alerting rules, and it took about twenty minutes to use. You give it synthetic series and assert which alerts fire and when:

- interval: 1m
  name: PDSCircuitOpen fires once the breaker is open
  input_series:
    - series: 'pybreaker_state{name="pds"}'
      values: "0x5 1x10"
  alert_rule_test:
    - eval_time: 4m
      alertname: PDSCircuitOpen
      exp_alerts: []
    - eval_time: 9m
      alertname: PDSCircuitOpen
      exp_alerts:
        - exp_labels: { severity: warning, team: interop, name: pds }

There are nine cases now. The one I would keep if I could only keep one is this:

- name: with no series exported the rule is silent, which was the bug
  input_series:
    - series: 'up{job="transform"}'
      values: "1x20"
  alert_rule_test:
    - eval_time: 15m
      alertname: PDSCircuitOpen
      exp_alerts: []

That is the repo as it actually stood. The rule is right, there is nothing for it to read, and the test documents that this is indistinguishable from health.

promtool check rules and promtool test rules now run as a CI job, so the rules are exercised on every pull request rather than during the first outage.

Watching it fire, rather than trusting the test

A promtool test proves the expression is right. It does not prove the pipeline produces the series under real conditions, so the last step was to break the thing on purpose:

make break-pds

That stops pds-client, sends eight messages two seconds apart, and prints the gauge after each one. Every message returns 200 throughout, which is the whole point: enrichment has stopped, the stored demographics are now whatever arrived in the message, and the front door is reporting success.

The first time I ran it against the real stack, the gauge read 0 after all eight messages. The breaker never opened.

The fix that still could not fire

The unit test for the gauge passed because it drove the breaker with an
ordinary function. The real PDS call is async, and I had wrapped it with pybreaker's decorator:

@pds_breaker
async def _call() -> dict | None:
    ...

pybreaker's only async support is for Tornado, and its README does not mention asyncio at all. On an async def function, the decorator calls it, gets a coroutine object back, and records a success. The request fails later, when the coroutine is awaited, outside the breaker. The running service had logged 16 PDS failures, and the breaker had counted none of them.

The fix is pybreaker's calling() context manager, which wraps the awaited block itself:

async def _call() -> dict | None:
    with pds_breaker.calling(), PDS_LATENCY.labels(outcome="success").time():
        resp = await http.get(...)

There is now a test that goes through the real async path with PDS failing. It fails against the old code.

It's the same shape as the getattr bug, one layer further down. The rule was right, the gauge was right, the listener was right, and the breaker they all depended on was never told anything had gone wrong. Every layer had a test and every test passed.

With the fix in, the breaker opens on the fifth message, and PDSCircuitOpen goes to Firing once the rule's two minutes have passed.

I had also worried that for: 2m could never be satisfied, because the
breaker's reset_timeout is 30 seconds and I expected the state to bounce between open and half-open. My first check of that went through the same synchronous test path, so it measured nothing real. In the running stack, the gauge held flat at 1 for twelve minutes, until I brought PDS back. pybreaker only moves to half-open when a call arrives after the timeout, and that trial call closes or reopens it in the same moment, so a ten-second scrape never sees it.

There is a second script for the other failure path, and writing it corrected something in my own plan for this article. The plan said to "stop the transform service mid-burst and show the DLQ". That does not work. The dead-letter folder is written by transform, so stopping transform means nothing writes to it at all: ingest logs the failure and answers 200 with forwarded: false. To fill the dead-letter folder you have to break what transform writes to, which is HAPI FHIR. make break-fhir does that.

Its first real run found one more. Every dead-letter write failed with
PermissionError. The service runs as an unprivileged user, and the Docker volume mounted over its dead-letter folder belonged to root, because the image never created that folder. So the messages the folder exists to keep were the ones being lost. The image now creates the folder, owned by the service user, and Docker copies it into a new volume when the volume is first created.

The panels, which I nearly forgot

Four new metrics and, for most of a day, no way to see any of them. The Grafana dashboard had six panels, and not one showed the breaker state, the dropped fields, the invalid NHS numbers or the write identity.

That is a fairly pointed thing to nearly ship in an article about not being able to see things. The series existed, and the alerts worked, and the place people actually look had not changed at all. There are ten panels now.

The one a reader found

Kevin Mayfield, who does health integration and data architecture for a living, read Part 3 and pointed out something I had not considered at all.

I had just shipped a fix that keys patient identity on the NHS number, as a conditional update. He pointed out that his trust is near the Scottish border, and that a Scottish CHI number sometimes arrives in the NHS Number field. More than that: a patient's NHS number can change when they move between the Scottish and English NHS.

Which means the identity key I had just built the whole write path around is not stable.

I tested it. Same patient, same hospital number, two messages with different NHS numbers:

message 1 request : PUT Patient?identifier=...nhs-number|1111111111
message 2 request : PUT Patient?identifier=...nhs-number|9000000009
same target?      : False
local MRN in both : L12345, L12345

Two records. The hospital number is identical in both messages and is simply not looked at. Nothing counts it, nothing alerts on it, and the FHIR server returns 200 twice.

That led somewhere I should have gone in Part 3. If the NHS number is the identity key, is it ever validated?

9000000009   checksum valid: True   accepted: True
1111111111   checksum valid: True   accepted: True
1234567890   checksum valid: False  accepted: True

No. An NHS number carries a Modulus 11 check digit, and the NHS Data Dictionary is unambiguous about it: "The check digit is validated using the Modulus 11 algorithm, and the use of this algorithm is mandatory." Multiply the first nine digits by 10 down to 2, sum, take the remainder modulo 11, and subtract from 11. A result of 11 means a check digit of 0, and "If the result is 10 then the NHS NUMBER is invalid and not used".

I was not running it. 1234567890 was being accepted as an NHS number and used to match a patient.

This is also a partial answer to Kevin's CHI point, which is why it is worth doing beyond tidiness. A CHI number is also ten digits, and it will not satisfy the NHS check digit. So a sending system supplying CHI numbers in the NHS Number field now shows up as a rate on nhs_number_invalid_total rather than as silently mismatched patients.

An identifier that fails the check is still kept on the resource, because the sender sent it and dropping it loses information. It is just never used to look a patient up or to match an existing record. A wrong identity is worse than no identity.

Writes with nothing to match on are now counted as patient_write_total{identity="none"}, and there is an alert when that passes a tenth of writes.

What none of this catches

The thing Kevin actually described is not a metric problem.

Counting writes with no identity tells you when matching is degrading. It does not tell you that the same person has arrived twice under two different NHS numbers, because from inside a single message that looks completely normal. Both messages are valid, both have good check digits, both write successfully.

Catching that needs a matching step, which is what he does:

I have a scoring system based on identifier, date of birth, gender, name and postcode. I weight MRN and NHS the highest, then DOB.

A demographic query first, then a weighted score across several fields, rather than trusting one identifier. He also raised the fetus and baby case, where a newborn may not have its own NHS number yet, which breaks identifier-first matching in a different direction.

That is a substantial piece of work, and it is not in this week's change. What this week does is make the conditions that feed it visible, so when the matching goes in there is something to measure it against.

Worth stealing

Test your alert rules. They are the only code in the repo that runs exclusively during an incident, which makes them the least exercised and the most load-bearing. promtool test rules exists and takes an afternoon to adopt.

Assert the series exists, not just that the rule is right. My rule was correct the whole time. The failure was one level below it, and no amount of reviewing the expression would have found it.

Watch for silent fallbacks in monitoring code: getattr with a default, or a synchronous decorator around an async function. Both fail by doing nothing, in the thing that is supposed to tell you about silent failures. My gauge read zero for the same reason the alert read quiet.

Count the successes you are unsure about. Error rates are the easy half. patient_write_total{identity="none"} counts requests that returned 200 and did something I would rather they had not.

Export the metric and add the panel in the same change. I had the series, the alert and the rule test before I noticed the dashboard still showed the same six panels it had in week one. A metric nobody has a graph for is halfway back to where this started.

Where AI helps here, and where it doesn't

I built this project with Claude Code. This week I had it write the metrics, the promtool tests and the break scripts, then made it prove each one against the running stack, not the code.

Writing the listener, the metrics and the promtool cases was quick. The useful part was the step before: starting the service, scraping /metrics and reading the list of what was actually there, rather than reading the alert file and the service code and believing they lined up. They had not lined up for weeks, and both halves looked correct on their own.

It also wrote the async decorator bug, and the first timing check that went through the same synchronous path. Both were caught the same way, by running the real stack and reading what it did.

Four weeks in, the pattern is stable enough to state plainly. Every finding in this series has come from running the thing, and the two most valuable have come from people who read it and knew more than I did about the domain. Neither of those is a code review.

What I'd do differently

I would have written the alert rule tests at the same time as the alert rules, in the first week. Not because the rules were wrong, but because writing the test is what forces you to produce the series, and producing the series is what I had skipped.

I would also have written the break scripts first. make break-pds is about thirty lines, and it is the only thing here that tests the whole chain, from a stopped container through to a rule evaluating in Prometheus. Everything else in this article tests one layer and assumes the next one. I would also have run it before tagging this part, not after.

And I would have remembered that fixing the code does not fix the data it already wrote. The demo database held 996 copies of the same test patient from before Part 3's conditional update. The conditional update then refused, correctly, to pick one, with the 412 the FHIR spec requires. I reset the demo database. A trust can't, and that is where the matching work Kevin described begins.

Sources

  • NHS Data Dictionary: NHS NUMBER, including the Modulus 11 check
  • Prometheus: unit testing rules
  • Prometheus: alerting rules
  • pybreaker on PyPI
  • pybreaker README: the calling() context manager and Tornado-only async support
  • FHIR R4: conditional update, including the 412 on multiple matches
  • Docker: populating a volume from a container
  • prometheus_client for Python
  • The code for this article, tag part-4

Next

Part 5, on 11 November, is security and compliance, which has a backlog of its own: two documents in this repo describe a DataClass tag applied by a Terraform block that is commented out.

Which of your alert rules has never fired, and do you know whether that is good news?

This is a personal project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NHS England or any NHS organisation. It uses the public PDS FHIR sandbox and synthetic test data only. Views are my own.

articles.title: Why Predicting Winner Models Breaks AI Routers
articles.description: Most multi-model routers treat dispatch as a winner-take-all classification problem. A study across 25 benchmarks shows why that destroys performance, and how outcome regression fixes it.
articles.body_html:
If you run an agent workflow in production, you have almost certainly thought about building a model router.

Frontier models cost twenty to fifty times more than compact reasoning models. For three-quarters of your daily tasks, a smaller model running on commodity infrastructure produces an identical result. The obvious architecture is to place a lightweight classifier in front of your gateway: examine the incoming prompt, predict which model will win the task, and dispatch the request to the cheapest candidate capable of solving it.

Almost everyone implements this as a standard classification head. You take historical run logs, mark the model that succeeded with the lowest latency or lowest token cost as the winner, and train a model to output that label.

That setup looks clean on paper, yet these routers regularly degrade in production. They route delicate multi-step tool calls to brittle models that crash, and they fail to beat a simple fallback policy that always calls a single frontier model.

A comprehensive study from researchers at the National University of Singapore, Cardinal AI Lab, UC Berkeley, and HKUST explains why this happens. Their paper, titled "Route Anything: A Study of Model and Policy Routing for General-Purpose AI Systems" (arXiv:2611.05275), evaluates routing across 25 benchmarks, spanning 374,401 scored runs across 452 candidate model configurations.

Their central finding dismantles the standard way engineers build model routers: training a router to predict winners penalizes the very capabilities you want to preserve.

The winner-label trap

The flaw in standard model routing lies in how training targets are constructed.

In multi-model systems, tasks are rarely exclusive. On a large fraction of typical inputs, several different candidate models can solve the problem correctly. If Model A, Model B, and Model C all succeed, your logging pipeline needs a rule to pick a single winner label for training.

Most pipelines use an operational tie-breaker, such as execution latency or token consumption. If Model A finished in 1.8 seconds while Model B took 4.2 seconds, Model A is labeled the winner.

The router paper ran this comparison on robotic manipulation tasks where multiple control policies operated across thousands of scenes. A latency tie-break decided 94 percent of the training labels. Out of 31,408 successful training runs, 24,556 successful trajectories were turned into negative targets.

By training a classifier to predict a single winner, the router was penalized whenever it predicted a capable policy that took slightly longer to finish. The classifier learned to prioritize fast, aggressive candidates that failed when the scene became difficult. When evaluated on test scenes, the winner-label classifier achieved only 42.8 percent task success.

When the researchers replaced the winner classifier with per-candidate outcome regression, predicting the expected success rate of each candidate independently, task success jumped to 71.6 percent on the identical training scenes and architecture.

When you predict outcomes, a candidate that succeeds reliably remains a positive signal regardless of whether another model solved the task three hundred milliseconds faster.

The benchmark baseline illusion

Another persistent problem in the model routing literature is the claim that small routing models easily outperform frontier models on general reasoning.

The paper uncovers an evaluation artifact that inflates router gains across published papers. In many benchmark evaluations, a candidate model is admitted to the fixed baseline only if it has a recorded score on every single test input. If a frontier model like Opus missed eleven out of 1,122 evaluation items due to transient network timeouts or provider rate limits, the baseline drops that model entirely and falls back to a weaker candidate.

On an 11-benchmark evaluation suite, this missing-data rule caused the pooled baseline score to drop from 68.30 to 65.52. That drop turned a 0.40 point deficit for the router into an apparent 2.38 point gain.

When the researchers evaluated candidates on matched test inputs, giving every model an identical fallback for missing items, the gap closed. Across 16 general benchmarks spanning text, vision, audio, and code, learned routers beat the single best fixed candidate by 0.3 points (79.98 versus 79.68).

If your goal is to beat the accuracy of the best frontier model on text reasoning, an upstream prompt router will rarely provide a significant edge.

Where routing actually pays off

The study demonstrates that routing delivers massive returns when applied to cost efficiency and cross-environment adaptation rather than benchmark point-chasing.

Across four production-style testbeds, dynamic routing improved compute and token efficiency by an average factor of 8.82 over calling a reference frontier model. When the router was calibrated to maintain a strict quality floor, it successfully routed straightforward queries to cheap models while reserving expensive models for high-variance inputs.

A second major gain appears when candidate models have complementary physical or environmental strengths. In robotic manipulation tests across clean and randomized environments, the best single policy achieved 70.45 percent success. A scene-aware router directed clean scenes to one policy (PatchWAM) and cluttered, randomized scenes to another (ME-Dex). The combined system reached 71.55 percent success while reducing policy execution time by 24 percent.

The efficiency gain was real because the router was not trying to guess whether one text model understood a pun better than another. It was dispatching tasks based on structural scene conditions where different architectures had distinct operating boundaries.

The retry fallacy

Many agent frameworks combine routing with fallback retries. If the primary routed model fails to complete an agent step or generate valid JSON, the gateway automatically retries the task using a larger frontier model.

The paper examined 42 ordered model pairs to measure how models perform when called as secondary fallbacks. In every single pair, the secondary model succeeded far less often on retried inputs than its normal baseline score suggested. The median success ratio on retries was 0.49.

When an initial model fails on an input, that failure acts as an informational filter. The remaining tasks are not an average sample from your production distribution; they are the pathological edge cases, ambiguous instructions, and contradictory tool schemas.

If your frontier model has an 80 percent success rate on raw traffic, you should expect it to succeed on less than 40 percent of the requests that failed on your primary model. Designing gateway timeouts and budgets around raw baseline accuracy guarantees cascading latency spikes.

Practical rules for gateway routing

If you are building an AI gateway or an agent dispatcher, the data from the Route Anything study suggests four engineering adjustments:

First, stop training winner classifiers. Train per-model regressors that estimate the probability of success or expected task score for each candidate independently. Select the cheapest candidate whose expected score meets your application threshold.

Second, test routing logic against a strictly matched baseline. Run both your router and your candidate models on the exact same set of historical requests, with identical handling for missing items. If a router paper does not guarantee matched test sets, assume the headline gain is an artifact of dropped baseline candidates.

Third, route for cost reduction and domain handoffs, not for frontier text accuracy. Use routing to offload high-volume boilerplate tasks to compact models, or to switch between specialized policies like document parsers and code interpreters. Expecting a small classifier to consistently pick a smarter text model than GPT-4 or Claude on open-ended reasoning is a losing bet.

Fourth, discount your retry assumptions by half. When sizing execution budgets for secondary fallbacks, calculate costs assuming the fallback model will fail twice as often as its public benchmark suggests.

That keeps the gateway fast, prevents brittle candidate loops, and protects the token budget when things go sideways.

articles.title: 133,334 Projections for 66,667 Receipts
articles.description: A Count() I added for a log line was re-running my whole LINQ query. I made the projection count itself to catch the double enumeration, then fixed it in one line.
articles.body_html:
A reporting method on a dashboard endpoint started showing up in the traces twice as heavy as the numbers it returned could explain. It pulled a filtered set of orders, logged how many there were, then summed them. Two cheap-sounding operations. The profiler disagreed, and the line it kept landing on was the one I'd never have circled: a Count() call I'd added for a log message.

Here's the shape of what I had.

void Report(IEnumerable<Receipt> receipts)
{
    logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} receipts", receipts.Count());

    double total = 0;
    foreach (var r in receipts)
        total += r.Total;

    logger.LogInformation("Total {Total:C}", total);
}

Looks like it touches the data twice, which it does, but that's not the expensive part. The expensive part is where receipts came from. It wasn't a list. It was a LINQ pipeline someone handed down the call chain:

var receipts = orders
    .Where(o => o.Region == "EU")
    .Select(o => new Receipt(o.Id, double.Parse(o.RawAmount) * 1.2));

That expression doesn't contain any receipts. It's a recipe for producing them, and it produces them fresh every single time something enumerates it. Count() enumerates it once to count. The foreach enumerates it again to sum. Same recipe, run top to bottom twice, filter and parse and allocate on both passes. The log line I thought was free was re-running the entire query.

Making the query admit it

I didn't want to argue from the profiler's vibe, so I made the projection count itself. Every time the Select runs, it bumps a counter. If the pipeline runs twice, the counter can't hide it.

int projected = 0;

IEnumerable<Receipt> Pipeline(IEnumerable<Order> orders) =>
    orders
        .Where(o => o.Region == "EU")
        .Select(o =>
        {
            Interlocked.Increment(ref projected);
            var amount = double.Parse(o.RawAmount);
            return new Receipt(o.Id, amount * 1.2);
        });

Then I ran the two-pass consumer against it and compared it to the obvious fix: enumerate once into a List, then ask the list whatever you want. Two hundred thousand source rows, a third of them in the EU bucket, so 66,667 matches. Best of seven, JIT warmed first. This is a container, not a lab bench, so I trust the projection count (it's exact) more than the millisecond.

// two passes: Count() then foreach, straight off the pipeline
var count = receipts.Count();
double total = 0;
foreach (var r in receipts) total += r.Total;

// one pass: materialize, then count and sum the list
var list = receipts.ToList();
double total = 0;
foreach (var r in list) total += r.Total;

Source rows:        200,000
EU rows (expected): 66,667
Results agree:      True (66,667 receipts)

enumerate twice  projections:    133,334   best:    12.2 ms
materialize once projections:     66,667   best:     7.2 ms

Projection ratio: 2.00x
Time ratio:       1.69x

Exactly double. 133,334 projections to produce 66,667 receipts, because every receipt got built, filtered, and parsed twice and half of them thrown away the first time around. The wall clock didn't quite double, which is the honest part: parsing and allocating are most of the cost here but not all of it, so the second pass adds about two-thirds again rather than a clean 100%. The ratio you'll see depends entirely on how heavy your Select is. Mine's a double.Parse. If yours hits a database, "twice" stops being a benchmark curiosity and becomes two round trips.

The fix is one call, and so is the trap

Materializing with ToList() collapses it back to one pass. The consumer can count the list, enumerate the list, index into the list, all for free, because a List<T> is results, not a recipe. If a method is going to look at a sequence more than once, it should own a materialized copy rather than a lazy expression it doesn't control.

The caveat, and it's a real one: ToList() is also how you turn a lovely streaming, bounded-memory pipeline into a full buffer in RAM. If the sequence is huge, or infinite, or you're deliberately streaming it so you never hold all of it at once, materializing is the bug and single-pass enumeration is the feature. The honest rule I land on is about intent. If I'm going to touch a sequence exactly once, left to right, I leave it lazy. The moment a method both counts and iterates, or iterates twice, I either materialize at the top or change the signature to demand a materialized type and push the decision to the caller.

That second option is the one I actually reach for in library-ish code:

void Report(IReadOnlyCollection<Receipt> receipts)   // not IEnumerable
{
    logger.LogInformation("Processing {Count} receipts", receipts.Count);
    // ...
}

IReadOnlyCollection<T> has a Count property, no enumeration required, and the type itself tells every caller "I'm going to treat this as a finished collection." You stop guessing whether the thing you were handed is a list or a time bomb, because the parameter won't accept the time bomb.

Here's the complete runnable sample if you want to watch the counter tick. Drop it in a net10.0 console project and dotnet run -c Release.

using System.Diagnostics;

Order[] source = BuildOrders(200_000);

int _projected = 0;

IEnumerable<Receipt> Pipeline(IEnumerable<Order> orders) =>
    orders
        .Where(o => o.Region == "EU")
        .Select(o =>
        {
            Interlocked.Increment(ref _projected);
            var amount = double.Parse(o.RawAmount);
            return new Receipt(o.Id, amount * 1.2);
        });

static (int count, double total) SummarizeTwice(IEnumerable<Receipt> receipts)
{
    var count = receipts.Count();          // pass one
    double total = 0;
    foreach (var r in receipts)            // pass two
        total += r.Total;
    return (count, total);
}

static (int count, double total) SummarizeOnce(IEnumerable<Receipt> receipts)
{
    var list = receipts.ToList();          // the only enumeration
    double total = 0;
    foreach (var r in list)
        total += r.Total;
    return (list.Count, total);
}

const int Runs = 7;

_ = SummarizeTwice(Pipeline(source));
_ = SummarizeOnce(Pipeline(source));

_projected = 0;
var twiceProjected = 0;
var bestTwice = double.MaxValue;
(int count, double total) twiceResult = default;
for (int i = 0; i < Runs; i++)
{
    _projected = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    twiceResult = SummarizeTwice(Pipeline(source));
    sw.Stop();
    bestTwice = Math.Min(bestTwice, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    twiceProjected = _projected;
}

var onceProjected = 0;
var bestOnce = double.MaxValue;
(int count, double total) onceResult = default;
for (int i = 0; i < Runs; i++)
{
    _projected = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    onceResult = SummarizeOnce(Pipeline(source));
    sw.Stop();
    bestOnce = Math.Min(bestOnce, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    onceProjected = _projected;
}

var euCount = source.Count(o => o.Region == "EU");

Console.WriteLine($"Source rows:        {source.Length:N0}");
Console.WriteLine($"EU rows (expected): {euCount:N0}");
Console.WriteLine($"Results agree:      {twiceResult == onceResult} ({twiceResult.count:N0} receipts)");
Console.WriteLine();
Console.WriteLine($"enumerate twice  projections: {twiceProjected,10:N0}   best: {bestTwice,7:F1} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"materialize once projections: {onceProjected,10:N0}   best: {bestOnce,7:F1} ms");
Console.WriteLine();
Console.WriteLine($"Projection ratio: {(double)twiceProjected / onceProjected:F2}x");
Console.WriteLine($"Time ratio:       {bestTwice / bestOnce:F2}x");

static Order[] BuildOrders(int n)
{
    var regions = new[] { "EU", "US", "APAC" };
    var orders = new Order[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        orders[i] = new Order(i, regions[i % 3], (10 + i % 500).ToString());
    return orders;
}

record struct Order(int Id, string Region, string RawAmount);
record struct Receipt(int Id, double Total);

The one that bites in production isn't even this tidy. It's an IEnumerable<T> returned from a repository, passed through three methods, and somewhere along the way one of them calls .Any() to null-check and another does the real loop, and now your query ran twice and nobody wrote the word "twice" anywhere. What's the sneakiest double-enumeration you've found in your own code? I'd like to collect a few.

— still counting things nobody asked me to count

articles.title: Your AI agent skills are probably out of date. Mine were. Here's how I handled it.
articles.description: My old agent skill was one long file and it told every agent I used to run MinIO for local S3. Then...
articles.body_html:
My old agent skill was one long file and it told every agent I used to run MinIO for local S3. Then the minio/minio repository on GitHub was archived, and the skill went on recommending it. The agents had no way to know. They just did what the file said.

Instructions for AI agents go stale the same way documentation does, except an agent acts on them without asking whether they're still true. So I rebuilt mine as dev-pops-skills, a set of agent skills built around one idea: every fact in them carries the date it was last checked, and something notices when that date gets old.

In this post:

  • what the skills are
  • how they stay fresh, which is most of the post
  • what happened when I measured whether agents actually use the skills (20 out of 31)

Seven small skills instead of one long file

dev-pops-skills is my DevOps defaults written down as seven small skills: Docker, CI/CD, Terraform, security scanning, shell scripting, whole-project setup, and one for writing and auditing the skills themselves. They work in Claude Code, Antigravity and any agent that supports the open Agent Skills format. An agent loads only the skill that matches the request, which matters because my old single file was so long the agents rarely followed it.

Each skill lists the defaults it applies without asking, such as pinned image tags and GitHub OIDC roles in place of stored AWS keys. It lists what needs a yes first: deleting volumes, pushing images, running terraform apply. And it ends with checks whose output the agent has to paste back, so "done" means something I can read.

Every fact has a date on it

The repo notices when something goes stale, then an agent updates it with me.

Every external fact a skill relies on lives in a sources.md file next to it, with the link it came from and the date it was checked. That covers image tags, action versions, install paths and whether a project still exists. Facts are looked up online when they're written, never from the model's memory. The MinIO fix, for example, is one row:

| MinIO's GitHub repo `minio/minio` is archived. | https://github.com/minio/minio | 2026-09-26 |

Four things watch those facts:

  1. Skills expire. Each skill records when it was last fully re-checked, and the validator that runs on every pull request warns once that's more than 90 days ago.
  2. A weekly job checks every pin. Every Monday a GitHub Action confirms that each pinned image tag still exists on Docker Hub, and that each pinned GitHub Action exists, isn't archived and isn't a major version behind. On any drift it opens an issue.
  3. Dependabot opens pull requests for minor and patch updates to base images. It ignores major versions on purpose: moving the templates to a new Node major changes a default, and that needs a decision from me, not an automatic PR.
  4. Real projects report back. When an agent hits a broken or missing template while working in one of my projects, it fixes the project with the smallest change it can, then files a finding in the repo's contributions/ folder with a reproduction. It never names the client, and a CI check fails the build if a name from my private list slips through.

When the weekly issue opens, or findings pile up, I ask an agent to "audit the skills". The skill-authoring skill takes over. It re-checks each fact online and shows me a table of what changed before it edits anything. It applies only the fixes I approve, then bumps the skill's version, adds a changelog entry, updates the dates and opens a pull request. Nothing changes without my approval, and main only accepts a PR that passes five CI checks.

The same loop caught my own tooling: when I moved from Gemini CLI to Antigravity, the install paths changed, and that went in with a source and a date like everything else.

The checks need checking too. I once added two linters set to warn without blocking, so I could fix the existing files first, and they showed a green tick on every run. The logs said both had been failing all along, because GitHub shows a non-blocking failure as a pass. So once in a while I open the logs of the checks themselves instead of trusting the tick.

I checked whether the agents actually use them

A skill only helps if the agent decides to load it, and it decides from a one-paragraph description. So I wrote 31 requests the way I'd phrase them, each paired with the skill that should load, plus four that should load none. A script sends each one to a headless Claude Code that has only these skills and records which skill it loads first.

I didn't want to install the CLI on my laptop for this, so the whole test runs in a throwaway Docker container. The image installs Claude Code from Anthropic's signed apt repository, and the build fails if the signing key's fingerprint doesn't match the one in their docs. I logged in once inside the container, the login lived in a Docker volume, and the repo was mounted read-only so nothing in there could change it:

docker run --rm -v dev-pops-eval-home:/home/eval -v "$PWD:/repo:ro" dev-pops-eval ./scripts/eval-triggers.sh --run

When I was done, I deleted the volume and the image, and my machine was back where it started.

The first full run, on Haiku, got 20 of 31. No request loaded the wrong skill, and all four unrelated ones ("write a React component for a sortable table") correctly loaded nothing. Every miss loaded no skill at all.

Most of those misses were my test's fault. I had asked the agent to "tidy this Makefile" in a project with no Makefile, and it said so, which is the right answer. Each request now runs against a small stand-in project that has the files it mentions. One miss was real: "write a shell script that waits for Postgres" never loaded the scripting skill, and that description is next on my list.

The test also drained my Claude session. I wanted one fact from each run, which skill loaded first, but every request started a full agent session that kept going after it had loaded the skill. It explored the project, read the skill's reference files, and several runs wrote me careful plans for work I would never read. After one full run, I queued two more to measure variance, and eleven prompts into the first of them my five-hour usage window ran dry. A test about whether agents follow instructions had been spending my limit on agents following instructions very thoroughly. Now each run stops the moment a skill loads, gets read-only tools, and is capped at three turns and three cents. By default it runs a sample of nine prompts.

If you want to try it

These are my defaults: Node and TypeScript, Docker Compose, GitHub Actions, and AWS with Terraform. If yours differ, fork the repo and change them; the skill-authoring skill walks an agent through it, and the freshness checks come with it once you enable Actions on your fork (GitHub turns scheduled workflows off on forks).

The repo is poppyszn/dev-pops-skills, MIT licensed. If you found this useful, star it so the next updates show up in your feed, and share the post with whoever on your team keeps the agent instructions. I'd like to hear how other people keep theirs from going stale.

articles.title: How I Vet an Open-Source Dependency Before Betting On It
articles.description: Six checks that catch a repo which doesn't do what its docs claim — grep for the feature, read the doc's target branch, check the tier gate and the payment rail.
articles.body_html:
Originally published on my blog — read it there with the full context, code and updates.

I was handed a 1,306-line architecture spec for a partner program. It read like a
plan: consistent, cross-referenced, confident. It named a self-hosted
open-source engine as the attribution and commission layer, and it assumed three
things about that engine — that it spoke OIDC so my existing identity provider
could log partners in, that its commission rules covered the five shapes the
business needed, and that its white-label feature was shipped.

Ten minutes of curl and grep later, two of those were false and the third was
half-true. None of that is unusual. The README describes the product; the
repository describes the software. The gap between those two is exactly where
integration projects die — and it is cheap to measure before you write any code.

The problem, phrased as the question I'd actually search for

How do I know an open-source project does what its documentation claims before
I build on it?

A spec is a claim about other software. The more polished the spec, the more its
assumptions read like facts — this one cited sources, defined stable IDs, and had
a source-of-truth matrix. What it never did was check whether the engine down the
chain implemented the features being assigned to it. So before installing
anything, I went looking for those specific features.

What I tried first, and why it wasn't enough

1. Read the README end to end. It sells the pipeline well:
click → identity → event → attribution → commission → payout. It never once
says which authentication protocol the app speaks. For a feature you need,
silence isn't neutral — but an absent mention is easy to skim past when the rest
of the page is convincing.

2. Searched the web. Several of my queries returned nothing usable. The
project is a few months old and its SEO surface is thin. For software that's
fine — the source is the documentation. It just means the reading has to happen
in the repo, not in a blog post.

3. Found a 78 KB feature design doc and assumed the feature shipped. It was
labelled "FINAL, post-review", listed three reviewers, and carried a date. I took
that as proof. That was the worst inference of the three, and the easiest to check.

The six checks that actually settled it

1. Read the repo's vital signs before any feature claim 

curl -s -H "User-Agent: hermes" https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo> \
  | grep -E '"created_at"|"pushed_at"|"stargazers_count"|"forks_count"|"open_issues_count"|"archived"|"spdx_id"'

What came back: MIT, created 2026-04-23, last push 2026-09-10, 8 stars, 3 forks,
15 open issues, not archived. Read the same as: real, still moving, and very
small — one vendor, which also sells a hosted tier. Now I know how much of my
business I want resting on it before I start grading its features.

2. Grep for the feature instead of reading for it 

grep -in 'oidc\|sso\|saml' README.md ARCHITECTURE.md docs/*.md | wc -l

Zero hits. The app authenticates with its own magic-link sessions and
per-persona API keys; it does not speak OIDC at all. That one line of output
killed a phase of the plan — "put the portal behind our SSO provider" — which
would otherwise have surfaced weeks later, mid-integration, with a partner
already invited. Reading for a feature you can't find is how you lose an
afternoon; grepping makes the absence loud.

3. Read the target branch line at the top of a feature doc 

head -5 docs/white-label-custom-domains.md

Target branch: multi-tenant. The doc is a design for a branch that is not the
default branch — it describes work in flight, so the feature is not in the code
you would install. A finished-looking document with reviewers and dates can
document something unshipped. That isn't dishonesty; it's what design docs are.

4. Read the data model, not the feature list

The commission section named exactly two rule types — percent (with a recurring
flag) and fixed. The business spec had enumerated five. That gap isn't a bug;
it's a modelling job I'd have to do in configuration instead of expecting from
the product:

Spec assumed What the engine actually has
first-order bonus a fixed rule on the first event
event-specific rules (lead vs invoice_paid) one rule per campaign — so: two campaigns
recurring commission percent + recurring: true
percentage percent ✅
fixed fixed ✅

Two rule primitives, five behaviours — workable, but only if you design for it up
front instead of discovering it during implementation.

5. Check which paid tier gates the feature you need

For the database tool in the same stack, the edition table was blunt:

Feature I needed Community (free) Enterprise (paid)
API tokens, so I can automate it ✅ ✅
SSO / OIDC ❌ ✅
Page designer, hide branding, 2FA ❌ ✅

The thing I wanted for the partner-facing door (SSO) sits behind the commercial
gate, while the thing I wanted for automation (an API token) is free. Knowing
which side of the wall each requirement falls on changes the design — before
you've designed around it.

6. Check that the money rail works in your country

The payout model was stripe_connect | manual, and self-hosted mode was
documented as "operator manages out-of-band" — i.e. you move the money yourself.
Stripe Connect is not how Malaysian businesses pay partners, so that one line
decided the entire deployment shape: self-host mode, manual payouts, and event
ingestion pushed from my own order system rather than leaning on the provider's
payment integration. That line is never on a marketing page, and it mattered more
than any feature.

Then: ask the fallback question before you need it

"What if the feature I need isn't there?" For the missing SSO the answer was:
don't put login in the app, put it in front of the app. authentik's proxy
provider exists to protect "applications that do not support native
authentication protocols such as OIDC, SAML, or LDAP", and it injects
X-authentik-username and X-authentik-groups headers upstream, so the reverse
proxy can do the gating. That turned "no SSO support" from a disqualification
into an afternoon of config.

What I'd do differently

  • Write the requirement list first, then go look for it. Five lines — the features I need — and search for those. Starting from the README's feature list means grading the software on the vendor's exam.
  • Treat "a doc exists" as different from "a feature ships". Read the branch line.
  • Grep, don't read. Presence is cheap to prove; absence is the thing you're hunting.
  • Decide the fallback before the decision, so a missing feature becomes a design change rather than a surprise.
  • Pin the commit. This project's README says its API is "stable but unversioned" and there is no OpenAPI description anywhere in the tree. There's no contract to compile against, so the commit hash is the contract — the endpoints I use go into my own docs, and upgrades get a regression pass.

The result

Six checks and about ten minutes of curl and grep corrected all three faulty assumptions in the spec before a single line of integration code existed. The project stayed viable — but
reshaped: no OIDC, manual payouts, a pinned commit, and a plan that no longer
depends on a feature sitting on an unmerged branch.

The spec wasn't wrong to be optimistic. It was wrong to be unverified, and that's
the cheapest thing on the whole project to fix.

Building on a self-hosted stack, and want a second pair of eyes on whether
those features will actually be there when you integrate? That's the kind of
review I do.
