articles.title: I Built a Judge My AI Couldn't Influence. In 51 Runs, It Never Gave a B.
articles.description: I built an autonomous scientific discovery engine called RUMI. I let it run for up to 21 hours per...
articles.body_html:
I built an autonomous scientific discovery engine called RUMI. I let it run for up to 21 hours per question. Then I built a frozen external judge it had no way to influence, and graded 51 of its runs.

Zero A's. Zero B's. Forty-five C's. Six F's.

The finding isn't that an AI failed to discover things. The finding is exactly how its self-assessment failed, and what that means for anyone building agents that grade themselves.

What RUMI is

RUMI is a pipeline that takes a research question and searches the live literature. It builds a knowledge graph, mines gaps and anomalies, and generates hidden variables and causal mechanisms. It then runs a theory tournament, attacks its own winners adversarially, and refines them through a thirteen-stage "scientific courtroom." In its most ambitious mode, it rewrites its own source code. It's built by one person and runs in a terminal.

I ran it in full mode across eight domains: drug discovery, space astronomy, neuroscience, physics, materials science, mathematics, computer science, and general. Runs took anywhere from 20 minutes to 21 hours and 12 minutes. Each produced a structured report with papers, entities, gaps, anomalies, mechanisms, predictions, a tournament winner, and a self-assigned score.

The judge

RUMI scores itself on seven weighted dimensions (novelty, explanatory power, predictive power, falsifiability, evidence strength, mathematical rigor, simplicity) and assigns a grade from A to F. Like most self-scoring agents, it's generous.

So I wrote eval/harness.py: an external evaluator with six deterministic metrics, its own A-F scale, and a hash-chained append-only ledger so no one can quietly rewrite a past score. The engine is forbidden from touching the eval/ directory in its self-modification loop. The judge and the judged are separated by a wall.

The headline

Across 51 externally graded runs:

  • A: 0
  • B: 0
  • C: 45
  • F: 6

Mean external score: 52.0 out of 100. Mean self-score: 58.9. The engine's own report card said "B" about a dozen times. The judge said C forty-five times and F six.

The jitter

The easy reading is "the model is overconfident by about twenty points." That reading is wrong.

The average gap between self-score and external score is +1.1. On average, the engine is barely optimistic. The average hides a bimodal mess:

  • 26 of 51 runs scored themselves lower than the judge did.
  • 16 of 51 overshot the judge by 10 points or more.
  • The largest self-inflation was +38.0 (self 70.7, judge 32.7).
  • The largest self-deflation was -52.8 (self 0, judge 52.8).

The self-scorer isn't biased. It's uncalibrated: a noisy estimator with swings of 20 to 50 points and no reliable relationship to the external score. You can't use it as evidence, as a training signal, or as a stopping criterion. Self-assessment in an autonomous agent isn't a measurement. It's a narrative the agent tells about itself, and nothing in the score tells you whether that narrative is modest or wrong.

What I found when I went digging

It fetches real papers and then doesn't cite them. Each run pulls 100 to 105 papers from arXiv, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, and CrossRef, walks citation networks two hops deep, and enriches entities against about fifteen scientific APIs (UniProt, PDB, PubChem, ClinicalTrials, KEGG, Materials Project, and others). Yet the evidence_strength sub-score is 0 in all 67 scored runs, and the no_citations flag fires in all 51 externally graded runs. The reports contain no resolvable citations at all.

I checked that this isn't a detector blind spot. The harness reads summary_text from the report JSON, and 76 of the 78 run JSONs have that field. None contain a structured [N] citation. I also scanned the 60 raw .txt reports: no [N] markers, and no "References" or "Bibliography" section in any of them. I looked for other formats too. Author-year citations like (Smith, 2024) turned up zero hits in the reports I sampled. The few "et al." mentions were incidental references to well-known papers inside the narrative, not citations backing a claim. Nine JSONs contain a literal [1], but only inside prose, with no reference list for it to point to. Those are citation-shaped tokens, not citations.

I call this retrieval-reasoning dissociation. Retrieval is real and structurally upstream. Reasoning downstream is citation-free. The output looks grounded because the data is real, but the claims never touch it. It's the difference between a system that has read the literature and one that has only downloaded it.

Self-refinement is a coin flip. RUMI's --iterate mode runs the pipeline twice, analyzes its own weaknesses, and reruns. In one molecular-glue run, the score rose from 65.0 to 80.1. In another, on the same class of problem, it fell from 83.8 to 65.2. More compute on the same question helped about half the time.

Textbook science won novelty tournaments. At least six runs carried a NULL HYPOTHESIS CHECK: WARNING, which caps the score at 64. Winning theories included "ΛCDM Cold Dark Matter Halo" and "Standard ΛCDM with Peculiar Velocity Corrections." The standard cosmological model won a tournament meant to produce novel hypotheses.

Schema leaked into the narrative. One winning theory carried the literal variable name percolation_threshold_pc as its title. A raw code identifier made it all the way through to the story.

The system named its own process as a discovery. One drug-discovery run's winner was "Positive Feedback Loop in Research Focus," an abstract meta-process offered as the reason Alzheimer's candidates fail in late-stage trials.

Compute is not quality. The 21-hour-12-minute run, on a materials-science question, scored 60.6. A C. "Let it run overnight" is not a research strategy.

What this doesn't prove

I built both the engine and the judge, so this needs stating plainly.

First, "uncorrelated with the external score" means uncorrelated with my frozen six-metric judge, not with ground truth. The judge is deterministic and tamper-evident, but it is still my design. A harsh or miscalibrated judge would also produce zero A's.

Second, 51 runs across eight domains is a small, uneven sample. Of those, 48 predate the harness, so their external scores were backfilled into the archive rather than shipped inside each report.

Third, the judge's validation is thin. To check that the harness can reward good work at all, I built a synthetic control: a RUMI-shaped report with 5 real papers, [1] to [5] citations that resolve to those papers, cited claim sentences, a named winner, mechanism steps, and predictions. Through the same frozen harness it scored 68.6, a B, the first B the harness has ever produced. Its citation_validity and claim_support_rate were both 1.0, against 0 and null for RUMI. Its structure_completeness was 0.429, against about 0.14 for RUMI. So the harness does separate a well-cited, well-structured report from RUMI's output. But the control is something I constructed to fit the format, not a human-written scientific report, so it shows the judge can discriminate on citations and structure, not that its grades track scientific quality. A real human-written benchmark is the next test.

Fourth, one of the six metrics is effectively dead. score_consistency never fires on real RUMI data, because the reports store dimension scores as top-level keys (like novelty_score: 60) instead of under the sub-dicts the metric expects. The self-versus-external gaps in this article are unaffected, since they compare the two final scores directly. But the judge is running on five working metrics, not six, and I've documented the bug in the repo.

The diagnosis

The system retrieves real evidence and then narrates without it. Its self-score tracks nothing external, and its outputs look like science. Everything upstream of the gap (retrieval, graph, enrichment, computation) is real and often good. Everything downstream (claims, theories, scores) is unmoored. The engineering work lives in the gap between "looks grounded" and "is grounded."

What I got wrong along the way

I initially said the engine inflates its score by 14 to 22 points. That holds only for the top leaderboard rows. Across all 51 runs the mean gap is +1.1, with 26 runs under-reporting.

I initially said the external score ships inside every report JSON. That's the design intent, but the 48 pre-harness runs have it backfilled.

My first audit concluded "everything is theater." That applied to a small demo folder, not the real engine, which does retrieve, enrich, and verify mechanically. The failure is the disconnect, not an absence of capability.

Part two: the fix

The smallest fix I can think of is claim-citation binding at generation time. Every claim sentence in a generated theory must carry a citation index that resolves to a paper in that run's retrieved corpus. Claims without one are downgraded to "speculative" with a penalty, or removed.

The success criterion is frozen in advance: citation_validity and claim_support_rate must exceed 0.8 on the same topics, without degrading novelty_vs_archive or structure_completeness, as measured by the same harness. I'll publish the before and after, whichever way it goes. If it works, the pattern applies to any agent that narrates from retrieved data without citing it.

Reproduce it

Everything is open.

  • Engine: github.com/subhansh-dev/rumi
  • Dataset, frozen judge, ledger, and paper: github.com/subhansh-dev/rumi-public

Run it:

git clone https://github.com/subhansh-dev/rumi
cd rumi
python run_discovery.py "your research topic" --mode full

Reproduce a score:

cd rumi-public/Engine
python -m eval.harness ../Dataset/discovery_v2_<timestamp>.json

No API keys are included, and free-tier providers are documented in Engine/api_keys.md. The 86 eval tests pass and the ledger is hash-chained. If you find a flaw in the measurement, open an issue. That's the point.

articles.title: Turning Video into Line Art in the Browser with WebGL 2 and Sobel
articles.description: Depth maps and line art preserve different parts of a video. Depth describes spatial relationships;...
articles.body_html:
Depth maps and line art preserve different parts of a video. Depth describes spatial relationships; contours emphasize shape, composition, and visible changes in pose.

After adding depth-video conversion to Timeline Studio, my open-source browser video editor, I added a line-art asset generator. This version runs locally with WebGL 2 and Sobel edge extraction. It does not download or run a neural line-art model.

Source code · Try the editor

Here is how the image-processing pipeline connects to actual video editing: previews, trimmed clips, speed curves, source audio, encoding, and cancellation.

Two passes on the GPU

The pipeline is deliberately small:

Image or decoded video frame
          |
   Grayscale + 3x3 smoothing
          |
   Intermediate GPU texture
          |
   Sobel + soft threshold
          |
    Output canvas
          |
      PNG or WebM

The smoothing pass renders into a texture attached to a framebuffer. The edge pass samples that texture and draws to the output canvas. Intermediate pixels stay on the GPU rather than being read back into JavaScript between passes.

Shader programs, buffers, textures, and the framebuffer are reused across frames. That reduces setup work, although decoding and encoding still contribute to total processing time.

Convert to luminance, then smooth

The shader computes a weighted RGB luminance:

float gray(vec2 p) {
  return dot(
    texture(source, p).rgb,
    vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722)
  );
}

The first pass uses this weighted 3x3 kernel, divided by 16:

1  2  1
2  4  2
1  2  1

Smoothing suppresses some high-frequency texture before edge extraction. It is a tradeoff: small details can also become weaker.

Because detection operates on luminance, different colors with similar luminance may produce weak boundaries. Conversely, a shadow or reflection can produce a strong edge without marking an object boundary.

Extract Sobel gradients

The second pass estimates horizontal and vertical gradients:

Gx                  Gy
-1  0  1            -1 -2 -1
-2  0  2             0  0  0
-1  0  1             1  2  1

Their combined magnitude becomes the edge strength:

float gradient = length(vec2(
  c + 2.0 * f + i - a - 2.0 * e - g,
  g + 2.0 * h + i - a - 2.0 * b - c
));

The letters represent neighboring luminance samples. Each output pixel performs the same local calculation, which maps naturally to a fragment shader.

Make the parameters useful

The inspector exposes detail, line weight, and inversion. Defaults are 55% detail, 1x line weight, and black lines on white.

Detail maps to an edge threshold:

float threshold = mix(0.42, 0.035, detail / 100.0);
float ink = smoothstep(threshold * 0.5, threshold, gradient);
float value = inverted ? ink : 1.0 - ink;

Higher detail lowers the threshold, retaining weaker edges. The soft threshold avoids an abrupt binary transition around the cutoff. For busy footage, increasing detail can make the result less useful by retaining background texture.

Line weight changes the sampling distance. It uses the longest dimension as a 1080px reference:

const scaledThickness =
  thickness * Math.max(width, height) / 1080;

This helps keep the edge-sampling scale comparable across output sizes. It is not morphological dilation: changing the sampling distance also changes which details respond. The initial blur itself remains a one-pixel 3x3 neighborhood.

Preview and asset generation share one renderer

Both paths call the same implementation:

const renderer = createLineArtRenderer(canvas, width, height);
renderer.draw(media, options);
// Release resources when finished:
renderer.dispose();

The preview redraws a sampled frame when parameters or the local playhead time change. Asset generation traverses output frames through that same renderer.

Sharing the implementation reduces differences in thresholds, sampling, and inversion between preview and generated assets. It does not make processing instantaneous.

Output dimensions preserve aspect ratio, cap the longest edge at 1080 by default, avoid enlarging smaller media, and normalize dimensions to even numbers.

Video has to follow the timeline's clock

A selected clip may already be trimmed or retimed. Sampling the original file from zero would produce the wrong result.

There are separate coordinates for output time, clip-local time, and source-media time. For constant speed:

sourceTime = sourceIn + clipLocalTime * speed

For speed curves, the implementation reuses the editor's mapping:

getVisualSourceTime(segment, localTime)

The generator outputs 24 fps. Each local sample time is i / 24; it is mapped to source time before decoding the frame. The processed frame is then encoded at its output timestamp.

Output frame time
       |
Source-time mapping, including trim and retiming
       |
Decode source frame -> draw contours -> encode output

Mediabunny handles media input and timestamp-based canvas sampling. The final frame duration is limited to the remaining clip duration.

24 fps is the output rate, not a claim of real-time generation speed. Actual throughput depends on the browser, hardware, source media, and encoder.

Normalize still-image orientation

One integration detail had nothing to do with Sobel: image orientation.

The image path decodes a Blob to an ImageBitmap, then draws it to a 2D canvas before uploading it to WebGL. ImageBitmap does not follow the same UNPACK_FLIP_Y_WEBGL behavior as the other upload path, so the intermediate canvas normalizes orientation.

Without that step, still images and video frames could disagree about which side is up.

Encode a reusable asset, with corresponding source audio

Images become PNG. Videos become WebM using VP9 at approximately 4 Mbps. When corresponding source audio exists, the output uses Opus at 192 kbps.

Audio preparation reuses the editor's source-audio and offline-mixing helpers so trimming and retiming follow the selected segment. This preserves the segment's corresponding source sound; it does not mix every music and narration track from the whole project.

The completed asset goes to My assets. It is not automatically inserted into the timeline, making it possible to retain the original and compare versions before placement.

Cancellation includes cleanup

An AbortController carries cancellation through source reading, frame processing, and output finalization. The renderer releases its textures, framebuffer, shaders, programs, and vertex buffer. Media input resources are disposed, and encoding is canceled when necessary.

Frame processing reports progress up to 99%. Finalization and the asset commit must finish before the UI reports completion. Processing the last frame is not the same as having a usable saved file.

What structural reference means here

Depth video and contour video provide complementary reference assets:

Asset Emphasizes
Depth video Relative depth and foreground/background layout
Line-art video Visible contours, composition, and changes in shape

A downstream generation workflow can use these only if it accepts the corresponding conditioning input and its preprocessing, timing, resolution, and frame-rate requirements are satisfied.

This feature creates the reference asset. It does not imply automatic integration with every image or video generator, nor guarantee that a generator will preserve the desired structure.

The current Sobel route also lacks semantic simplification and explicit temporal tracking. Fine textures, noise, and motion can make lines fluctuate across frames. A learned line-art model or additional temporal processing would need separate evaluation rather than being claimed as part of this implementation.

Try it or read the code

Open Effects -> Line art, select an image or video clip, adjust parameters, and generate the asset. The feature includes 13 interface languages and a mobile layout.

Implementation entry points:

  • src/lib/lineArt.js: renderer, source sampling, encoding, and cleanup
  • src/components/LineArtPanel.jsx: preview, controls, and job state
  • src/i18nLineArt.js: localized copy

If you work on browser graphics or video tools, I would welcome difficult examples: busy backgrounds, small contours, and fast motion are particularly useful for understanding where this approach needs improvement.

GitHub repository · Open the editor

Disclosure: I maintain the project discussed here. This article was drafted by an AI assistant using the current repository source and implementation notes.

articles.title: Late Chunking in Node: Embed the Whole Document, Then Cut, So 'Its' Still Means Berlin
articles.description: Naive chunking forgets what 'its' refers to. Late chunking embeds the whole document, then pools per chunk. Rebuilt in Node with Transformers.js.
articles.body_html:
• Book: AI That Reads
  • The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Take three sentences about Berlin, the same three Jina AI used to introduce late chunking:

  1. "Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany, both by area and by population."
  2. "Its more than 3.85 million inhabitants make it the European Union's most populous city, as measured by population within city limits."
  3. "The city is also one of the states of Germany, and is the third smallest state in the country in terms of area."

Split them into one chunk per sentence, embed each chunk on its own, and score each one against the query "Berlin". In Jina's run the cosine similarities came out at 0.849, 0.708 and 0.753. Sentences two and three are about Berlin. They just never say the word. "Its" and "The city" point back at a sentence the embedding model never saw.

Run the same three chunks through late chunking and Jina reports 0.850, 0.825 and 0.850. Same model, same chunks, same query. The only thing that changed is when the cut happens.

Why the middle chunk forgets Berlin

The usual RAG pipeline splits first and embeds second. Each chunk goes into the embedding model as a separate input, so the transformer's attention only covers the tokens inside that chunk. When the model reads "Its more than 3.85 million inhabitants", the word "Berlin" is nowhere in its input. The token "its" gets a vector for a generic possessive pointing at some large place. Mean pooling averages that into the chunk vector, and the result lands closer to "big European city" than to "Berlin".

The late-chunking paper by Günther, Mohr, Williams, Wang and Xiao (first posted September 2024, revised July 2025) states the problem plainly: chunk embeddings built this way "can lose contextual information from surrounding chunks". Pronouns make a clean demo, but the same failure hits "the company", "this endpoint", "the second option", or any reference whose antecedent landed in a different chunk.


Naive chunking: each strip is embedded alone, so the middle one loses its link to the city.

Run the transformer once, cut afterwards

Most embedding models already work in two stages. The transformer turns every token into a vector that has attended to every other token in the input. Then a pooling step (mean pooling, for the Jina v2 family) collapses those token vectors into one vector for the whole input.

Late chunking moves the chunker between those two stages. Algorithm 1 in the paper's current version goes like this:

  1. Decide chunk boundaries the way you already do: fixed size, sentences, or a semantic splitter. You get character spans.
  2. Tokenize the whole document and run the transformer over all of it, or as much as fits in the context window.
  3. Convert each character span into a token span.
  4. Mean-pool the token vectors inside each token span. One vector per chunk.

Step 2 is where "Berlin" gets in. The token vectors for "its" were computed with attention over the first sentence, so they already carry the reference. Pooling them per chunk keeps that context inside each chunk vector. Jina's write-up puts it this way: late chunking "still requires boundary cues", but those cues "are used only after obtaining the token-level embeddings."

Two properties make it cheap to adopt. The abstract says the method "works without additional training" (the paper also offers an optional fine-tuning recipe on top). And the output doesn't change shape: one vector per chunk at the same dimension, so your vector store stays as it is.


Late chunking: the model reads the whole document first, and the cut happens on the token vectors.

Rebuilding it in Node with Transformers.js

Transformers.js runs ONNX models in Node and the browser. Xenova/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en is the ONNX port of jina-embeddings-v2-small-en, a 33M-parameter, Apache-2.0 model with an 8,192-token window. Its tokenizer config declares a BertTokenizer with model_max_length set to 8192.

npm i @huggingface/transformers

Setup and the document:

// late-chunk.mjs
import {
  AutoTokenizer,
  pipeline,
  cos_sim,
} from '@huggingface/transformers';

const MODEL = 'Xenova/jina-embeddings-v2-small-en';
const MAX_TOKENS = 8192;

const chunks = [
  'Berlin is the capital and largest city of Germany, ' +
    'both by area and by population.',
  'Its more than 3.85 million inhabitants make it the ' +
    "European Union's most populous city, as measured " +
    'by population within city limits.',
  'The city is also one of the states of Germany, and ' +
    'is the third smallest state in the country in ' +
    'terms of area.',
];
const doc = chunks.join(' ');

const tokenizer = await AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL);
const extractor = await pipeline(
  'feature-extraction',
  MODEL,
  { dtype: 'fp32' },
);

Next, the token spans. The Transformers.js tokenizer options don't include an offset mapping like the Python tokenizers have, so this version counts tokens per chunk instead. The chunks are whole sentences joined by spaces, and a BERT tokenizer splits on whitespace before it breaks words into pieces, so tokenizing each chunk alone yields the same tokens as tokenizing the full document. The code still checks that the total token count matches what the model saw.

// Token span per chunk. Position 0 is [CLS].
function tokenSpans(chunks) {
  const spans = [];
  let cursor = 1;
  for (const text of chunks) {
    const ids = tokenizer.encode(text, {
      add_special_tokens: false,
    });
    spans.push([cursor, cursor + ids.length]);
    cursor += ids.length;
  }
  return { spans, total: cursor + 1 }; // + [SEP]
}

Now the late part. With pooling: 'none', the feature-extraction pipeline returns a tensor shaped [1, tokens, hidden], one vector per token. Pooling is a loop over a flat Float32Array:

function meanPool(data, dim, start, end) {
  const v = new Float32Array(dim);
  for (let t = start; t < end; t++) {
    const row = t * dim;
    for (let d = 0; d < dim; d++) v[d] += data[row + d];
  }
  for (let d = 0; d < dim; d++) v[d] /= end - start;
  return Array.from(v);
}

async function lateChunk(doc, chunks) {
  const { spans, total } = tokenSpans(chunks);
  if (total > MAX_TOKENS) {
    throw new Error(`${total} tokens, window is ${MAX_TOKENS}`);
  }
  const out = await extractor(doc, { pooling: 'none' });
  const [, seqLen, dim] = out.dims;
  if (seqLen !== total) {
    throw new Error(`spans cover ${total}, model saw ${seqLen}`);
  }
  return spans.map(([s, e]) => meanPool(out.data, dim, s, e));
}

And the comparison, with the naive version embedding each chunk as its own input:

async function naive(chunks) {
  const out = await extractor(chunks, { pooling: 'mean' });
  return out.tolist();
}

const q = await extractor('Berlin', { pooling: 'mean' });
const query = q.tolist()[0];
const before = await naive(chunks);
const after = await lateChunk(doc, chunks);

chunks.forEach((text, i) => {
  const a = cos_sim(query, before[i]).toFixed(3);
  const b = cos_sim(query, after[i]).toFixed(3);
  console.log(`naive ${a}  late ${b}  ${text.slice(0, 30)}`);
});

Run it with node late-chunk.mjs. I haven't run this exact script, so there's no output table here to copy. What to check is the direction: chunks two and three should climb toward chunk one. Jina's published numbers came from their own Python code, and an ONNX port won't match them to the decimal. The model page's own example shows fp32 and quantized weights already disagreeing in the third decimal (0.940 against 0.934). One deliberate difference from the paper: its Algorithm 1 folds [CLS] and [SEP] into the first and last chunk. To match that, start the first span at 0 and end the last span at total.

Does it hold beyond a three-sentence toy? Jina ran BEIR retrieval tasks with roughly 256-token chunks on the small model and published nDCG@10:

Dataset Avg doc length (chars) Naive Late No chunking
SciFact 1,498 64.20% 66.10% 63.89%
TRECCOVID 1,117 63.36% 64.70% 65.18%
FiQA2018 767 33.25% 33.84% 33.43%
NFCorpus 1,590 23.46% 29.98% 30.40%
Quora 62 87.19% 87.19% 87.19%

Quora documents average 62 characters, so each one fits in a single chunk and late chunking has nothing to add. In this table, the longer the documents, the bigger the gap. On TRECCOVID and NFCorpus, not chunking at all scored slightly higher than late chunking. Averaged over three models and four BEIR datasets, the paper reports nDCG@10 going from 52.2 to 54.0 with fixed-size boundaries and from 52.4 to 54.3 with sentence boundaries.

The 8,192-token wall

The trick only works if the document fits in one forward pass. Jina describes the v2 window of 8,192 tokens as "roughly ten standard pages of text". The model card says the model was trained at 512 tokens and uses a symmetric bidirectional variant of ALiBi to extrapolate to about 8k. That's why the code throws past MAX_TOKENS instead of letting anything truncate quietly.

For longer documents, the paper's Algorithm 2, "long late chunking", splits the token sequence into macro chunks of the maximum length, each overlapping the previous one by a set number of tokens. The overlap tokens provide context to the window but aren't reused in the output. The token vectors from all windows are concatenated, then pooled per chunk as before. The limit is still there: a chunk in window three can't see a definition that only appears in window one.

A few other costs come with it:

  • Edit one paragraph and you re-embed the whole document (or its window), because every chunk vector depends on the tokens around it.
  • You need token-level outputs. An endpoint that returns one pooled vector per input can't be late-chunked on your side. Jina's API has a late_chunking flag for jina-embeddings-v3: it concatenates your inputs and returns one embedding per input, with the total capped at 8,192 tokens per request.
  • It assumes mean pooling. Jina's follow-up post says it "can be applied to any long-context embedding model that uses mean pooling."

Late chunking vs Anthropic's contextual retrieval

Anthropic published Contextual Retrieval on September 19, 2024, about two weeks after the paper's first version. Their method sends Claude 3 Haiku the full document plus one chunk and asks for "a short succinct context to situate this chunk within the overall document". The answer, usually 50 to 100 tokens, gets prepended to the chunk before embedding and before BM25 indexing. Anthropic measured retrieval failures (1 minus recall@20) dropping 35% with contextual embeddings, 49% when contextual BM25 is added, and 67% with reranking on top. They estimated the one-time cost at $1.02 per million document tokens, assuming 800-token chunks, 8k-token documents and prompt caching.

That is one LLM call per chunk. A corpus of 50,000 chunks means 50,000 generation calls at index time, plus more whenever documents change. Late chunking needs one forward pass of a 33M-parameter model per document, with no generation step. Jina's follow-up calls the LLM route "expensive in terms of cost, time, and storage", which is fair to weigh while remembering who wrote it.

The paper ran both on one small example (Section 4.5): a fictional financial document and a question about ACME Corp's Q2 2023 revenue growth. For the chunk "It highlighted a 3% revenue growth over the previous quarter.", naive chunking scored 0.6343, late chunking 0.8516, and contextual embeddings 0.8590. That's a single example: it shows the two methods landing close on one chunk and says nothing about a full corpus.

Contextual retrieval has real advantages. The added context is text, so it helps BM25 too, and it travels with the chunk into the prompt you send the generator. You can also tune the prompt for your domain, for example with a glossary, as Anthropic suggests. Late chunking only changes vectors: your keyword index and your LLM still see the raw "Its more than 3.85 million inhabitants".

A reasonable order: if you host your own embedding model and your documents fit in 8k tokens, try late chunking first, because it costs one code change at index time. Reach for contextual retrieval when you need keyword search to benefit from the context, or when an index-time LLM bill is acceptable for your corpus size. Nothing stops you from doing both, though I haven't seen published numbers for the combination.

If this was useful

Late chunking is a small change at index time that plugs a recall leak most pipelines don't measure. AI That Reads is the book in my series about that whole layer in TypeScript: chunking, embeddings, vector search, and grounding answers in your own documents. If your retrieval looks fine in demos and misses on real questions, it's written for you.

It's book 2 of AI in TypeScript, five books from your first LLM call to agents in production: the whole series is here.

articles.title: Highlighting text without wrapping it in spans: the CSS Custom Highlight API
articles.description: The CSS Custom Highlight API is a browser API that lets you style arbitrary ranges of text by...
articles.body_html:
The CSS Custom Highlight API is a browser API that lets you style arbitrary ranges of text by registering Range objects in a Highlight, adding it to CSS.highlights under a name, and targeting that name with the ::highlight() pseudo-element. The DOM stays exactly as it was: no <span>, no <mark>, no extra nodes.

I ran into this while building a highlights-and-notes feature, and it changed how I think about the problem. This post covers why the old approach hurts, how the native API works, what support looks like today, and what you still have to build yourself.

What is wrong with wrapping highlights in spans?

For about fifteen years, the standard way to highlight text on a web page was to split text nodes and wrap the pieces in elements. mark.js wraps matches in <mark>. Rangy's highlighter and web-highlighter wrap them in <span>. It works, but it has costs:

  • You are editing a DOM someone else owns. In React, Vue or Svelte, the framework assumes it controls the nodes it rendered. If a library splits a text node and inserts a <span>, the next re-render can throw the highlight away, or fail outright when the framework tries to update a node that is no longer where it expected. If you've ever seen Failed to execute 'removeChild' on 'Node' after a third-party script touched your markup, you know what this looks like.
  • Overlapping highlights get messy. Two highlights that partly overlap need nested or split wrappers, and removing one means stitching text nodes back together correctly.
  • Selectors and styles change. p > a or :first-child can stop matching once extra elements appear. Copy and paste, textContent offsets and screen readers can all pick up the new structure.
  • Cleanup is your problem. Every "remove highlight" has to unwrap and normalize the nodes, or the DOM slowly fills with fragments.

None of this is a bug in those libraries. When they were written, wrapping was the only way to paint text.

How does the CSS Custom Highlight API work?

There are three pieces:

  1. Range: the same DOM Range you get from document.createRange() or new Range(), with a start and end inside text nodes.
  2. Highlight: a set-like object that holds one or more ranges.
  3. CSS.highlights: a registry (a HighlightRegistry, which behaves like a Map) where you give each Highlight a name. CSS then styles that name with ::highlight(name).

Here is the minimal version, with no library:

<p id="intro">The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.</p>

::highlight(note) {
  background-color: #fde68a;
  color: inherit;
}

if (typeof CSS !== 'undefined' && 'highlights' in CSS) {
  const textNode = document.getElementById('intro').firstChild;

  const range = new Range();
  range.setStart(textNode, 4);  // start of "quick"
  range.setEnd(textNode, 19);   // end of "fox"

  const highlight = new Highlight(range);
  CSS.highlights.set('note', highlight);

  // Later, to remove it:
  // CSS.highlights.delete('note');
}

Open DevTools after running this: the <p> still has a single text node. The browser paints the range, but nothing in the tree changed, so React (or anything else) can re-render the paragraph and the highlight is still painted as long as the range points at live nodes.

A few things the spec deliberately limits:

  • Only some properties apply inside ::highlight(): color, background-color, text-decoration and its longhands, text-shadow, and a handful of others. No padding, no border, no layout changes. That is the point: painting, not layout.
  • Ranges are live. If the DOM under a range changes, the range moves or collapses with it. That's great for small edits and a problem when a framework replaces the whole node (more on that below).
  • Highlights are not elements, so they get no events. There's no click on a highlight. You hit-test yourself: get the caret position from the pointer with document.caretPositionFromPoint() and check which range contains it, or compare the pointer against range.getClientRects(). A newer CSS.highlights.highlightsFromPoint() does this for you, but support is still partial (see below).
  • Priority. When highlights overlap, highlight.priority decides which one paints on top.

Which browsers support the CSS Custom Highlight API?

Checked on 3 November 2026 against MDN's browser-compat-data and the web-features "Custom highlights" entry:

Browser Highlight / CSS.highlights ::highlight() styling
Chrome / Edge 105 (2022) 105
Safari (macOS and iOS) 17.2 (December 2023) 17.2
Firefox 140 partial from 140 to 148: text-decoration works from 146, text-shadow from 149. Full from 149

The feature became Baseline "newly available" on 24 March 2026, when Firefox 149 shipped full ::highlight() support. Two caveats worth knowing:

  • In Safari, ::highlight() styles are ignored on text that also has user-select: none.
  • CSS.highlights.highlightsFromPoint() is only in Chrome 140+ and Firefox 150+ (Safari has it in preview), so keep a manual hit-test fallback.

If you need to support older browsers, there is no polyfill that keeps the "no DOM changes" property. You either fall back to wrapping, or you simply don't show highlights there.

What do you still have to build yourself?

The native API paints ranges. That's all it does. For a real highlights-and-notes feature, you still need:

  • Persistence. A Range is a pair of node references. It can't be saved to localStorage or a database. You need to serialize it into something stable.
  • Re-anchoring. When the page loads again, or the content was edited, or a framework re-rendered and replaced the text nodes, you have to find the text again and build fresh ranges. Character offsets alone break as soon as one word changes above your highlight.
  • Selection UI. Turning a user's selection into a highlight, and showing a toolbar or note editor next to it.
  • Hit-testing, as above, to open the note when someone clicks a highlight.
  • Framework lifecycle. Creating and destroying everything when a component mounts and unmounts, and not running on the server during SSR.

How does penciled build on top of it?

This is the part where I talk about my own project. I wrote penciled (penciled.org, JavaScript highlights & notes library), an MIT-licensed library of about 15 kB that does the list above on top of the Custom Highlight API. It never inserts elements into your content, and it has no wrapping fallback.

The default setup, with a built-in toolbar and note editor:

import { annotate } from 'penciled';
import 'penciled/styles.css';

const penciled = annotate('#article', {
  documentId: 'my-post',
  storage: 'local', // or 'memory', or your own adapter with load/save
});

const off = penciled.on('create', (annotation) => {
  console.log('created', annotation);
});

What it handles:

  • Persistence: localStorage by default, or a custom storage adapter (an object with load and save, plus optional create, update and delete) to sync with your backend. export() and import() move annotations around, and toW3C() converts them to the W3C Web Annotation format.
  • Anchoring: each annotation stores the quoted text, a short prefix and suffix, and start/end positions. On load, penciled tries the stored position, then exact matches of the quote, then a fuzzy match, and only accepts a result above a confidence threshold. If the text really is gone, the annotation isn't silently painted in the wrong place. It's marked as an orphan, fires an orphan event and stays in storage.
  • Notes: each highlight can carry a note, with a color and an indicator for highlights that have notes.
  • React: penciled/react exports an <Annotatable> component and a useAnnotations() hook. It's SSR-safe, because the instance is only created in an effect, and React can re-render the annotated content as often as it likes: 
import { Annotatable } from 'penciled/react';
import 'penciled/styles.css';

export function Post({ post, children }) {
  return (
    <Annotatable as="article" options={{ documentId: post.id }}>
      {children}
    </Annotatable>
  );
}
  • Headless: penciled/headless (about 6 kB) is the same engine without the UI. You get select events with the selected range and build your own toolbar: 
import { annotate } from 'penciled/headless';

const penciled = annotate('#article');

penciled.on('select', (context) => {
  if (!context || context.annotation || !context.editable) return;
  // position your own button using context.range.getBoundingClientRect()
  // then: penciled.create(context.range, { color: 'yellow' });
});

Highlights are registered as named highlights (penciled-<color>, penciled-<color>-noted, penciled-active), so you can style them with ordinary ::highlight() rules.

How does it compare to mark.js, Rangy and other options?

Honestly, it depends on what you need. These numbers come from my own comparison page, measured on 22 October 2026 (sizes are min+gzip):

Library How it paints Size Notes
mark.js wraps in <mark> ~6.2 kB Built for search-term highlighting, not saved annotations. Last release 8.11.1 in January 2018, still ~1.9M weekly downloads.
Rangy wraps in <span> ~22.7 kB A broad range/selection toolkit with a highlighter module. Latest 1.3.2.
web-highlighter wraps in <span> ~9.4 kB Persistence-oriented, and works back to IE11, which the native API can't.
@recogito/text-annotator separate overlay layer ~22.4 kB BSD-3, W3C annotation model, strong for collaborative and scholarly annotation.
Annotator.js jQuery-based — Last released in 2015. Hypothesis was originally built on it.
penciled CSS Custom Highlight API ~15 kB (~6 kB headless) No DOM changes, persistence and fuzzy re-anchoring built in. Pre-1.0, with far fewer users (~640 weekly downloads).

My rough guide:

  • Highlighting search matches on a static page? mark.js is small and battle-tested.
  • Need IE11 or very old browsers? You need a wrapping library such as web-highlighter or Rangy.
  • Collaborative, shared annotation with accounts and groups? Look at Hypothesis or Recogito.
  • Persistent personal highlights and notes in a modern app, especially one rendered by React, where you can't let a library rewrite your markup? That's the case I built penciled for.

If you only need to paint a few ranges, you don't need any library. The ten lines of native code above are enough.

Where can I try it?

Docs and a live demo are at penciled.org, and the source is on GitHub. There's also a free browser extension for Chrome, Firefox and Edge built on the same library, if you just want to highlight pages you read.

I'm Marcel Losso, the creator and maintainer of penciled, so weigh my comparison accordingly. Corrections and issues are very welcome on GitHub.

articles.title: Building a browser-based vocal splitter: decode locally, queue the job, delete the files
articles.description: Most tutorials about vocal separation start with "run Demucs on your GPU". That is a fine answer if...
articles.body_html:
Most tutorials about vocal separation start with "run Demucs on your GPU". That is a fine answer if you own the GPU, have Python set up, and are willing to wait. It is a bad answer for a web product, where the upload arrives over HTTP from a phone and the user expects a progress bar, not a CUDA error.

This post is about the middle part of that pipeline: what actually happens between "the user dropped a 40 MB MP4 on the page" and "here are two MP3s". I build Voice Remover, so the numbers and the failure modes below come from running it, not from a paper.

Step 1: decode in the browser, upload only the audio

The first decision that shapes everything else is where the file gets decoded. Server-side decoding of video is expensive, and it means a phone video sits on your storage before you know whether it is even usable.

Instead, the page uses the Web Audio API to decode the container and extract the audio track client-side. For an MP4 or MOV, the video stream never leaves the device. A 40 MB phone video can end up as a 3 MB audio upload, which changes both your bandwidth bill and the number of uploads that survive a flaky mobile connection.

// decode locally, re-encode to WAV, upload only that
const arrayBuffer = await file.arrayBuffer();
const audioCtx = new OfflineAudioContext(1, 1, 44100);
const decoded = await audioCtx.decodeAudioData(arrayBuffer);
// ...encode `decoded` to 16-bit PCM WAV, then POST the Blob

Two things bite here. decodeAudioData support differs by codec and browser, so M4A and MOV are the risky pair, not MP3. And you must re-encode rather than uploading the decoded buffer raw, because what you send to the separators wants to be a real audio file in a real container.

Step 2: an async job, not a long request

Separation takes tens of seconds. If you hold an HTTP request open for that, every proxy in the world will eventually time out on you, and you have no way to show progress.

The shape that works: the upload lands in object storage, a row is written to the database with a status, a message goes onto a queue, and the browser polls or subscribes for the status of that row. On Cloudflare that is R2 for the bytes, D1 for the row, and Queues for the handoff. The work runs on a Worker, which gets a fresh CPU budget per invocation and cannot be trusted to hold state in memory.

upload -> R2 -> D1 row (status=queued) -> Queue message -> Worker
Worker: claim row -> call separator -> write outputs to R2 -> status=done

The row is the only source of truth. Everything else is replaceable, which matters when your queue redelivers a message and you need the second worker to notice the job is already claimed.

Step 3: treat the third-party API as hostile

Separation itself is not something you want to run on a Worker. The model is heavy, and Workers are for glue. So the audio goes out to an inference provider — htdemucs on fal in our case — and comes back as two stems.

The lesson from production is that a third-party inference call is not a function call. It is a thing that can: accept your job and then lose it, return two stems with slightly different lengths, return silence for a file it did not like, or time out in a way that tells you nothing. So:

  • Store the provider's job id on your row before you await anything,
  • put a hard deadline on the polling loop rather than trusting the provider's own timeout,
  • and on any ambiguity, fail the row with a message a human can act on, rather than retrying three times and charging the user for a broken result.

Step 4: mix and encode on the edge, not in the model

The stems come back as raw audio and that is not what people want to download. Mixing and MP3 encoding happen back on a Worker. This separation of concerns is the whole reason the architecture is worth writing about: the model does one job, the plumbing does another, and you can change the model without touching the encoding.

Step 5: delete things on a schedule

Uploads get deleted when the job completes. Outputs get deleted after 24 hours. This is not only a privacy stance — although it is that too — it is cost control. Storage you forget about is the most common way a side project's bill climbs.

What this architecture actually costs you

Honest list of things that did not go smoothly:

  • Phone video is a menu of edge cases. A MOV from an iPhone is not the same container as an MOV from a screen recorder. Some files carry multiple audio tracks; pick one deliberately instead of letting the decoder guess.
  • The 10-minute file limit is a product decision disguised as a technical one. Longer files mean longer inference, more retries, more storage, and a worse free tier. Cutting at ten minutes kept the free tier honest.
  • Separation quality is a property of the recording, not the pipeline. Heavy reverb on the vocal, a live crowd, an old mono master — all of these leave traces in the instrumental. No amount of queueing fixes that, and users will tell you about it in the first week.
  • Backing vocals travel with the lead vocal. htdemucs gives you vocals and instrumental here; it is not a four-stem split. Anyone expecting drums and bass separately will be disappointed, so say so up front.

The one-line version

Decode in the browser, queue the job, keep one row as the source of truth, treat the inference provider as unreliable, encode at the edge, and delete on a schedule. If you are building anything that puts a heavy model behind a web form, the model is the easy part.

If you want to see the output rather than the diagram, the stem splitter shows the full two-track split, you can also isolate vocals from any song and get the acapella first, which is the view producers want, and there is a separate background music remover built on the same pipeline for speech-in-video use cases. The pricing page lists what the free tier actually covers, which is the number most people ask about first.

articles.title: Handover: I made three AI agents run an exit interview in team chat
articles.description: When someone leaves a team, the things they know usually leave with them. You find out three weeks...
articles.body_html:
When someone leaves a team, the things they know usually leave with them. You find out
three weeks later, when a cron job fails at 2 a.m. and the only person who knew the fix is
gone. The runbook says "TODO".

For the Flip the Switch hackathon I built
Handover. Three AI agents and the people involved run the handover in an ordinary chat
channel.

This post covers what it does, how to set it up from zero, and what I got wrong
along the way.

  • Repo:
    https://github.com/PinnacleCryptNG/handover

  • Demo video:
    https://youtu.be/yEJa8bV6z0M?si=0Y18zIxiUrBnbWsD

What it does

Handover has two rooms and three agents:

Room People Agents
payments-handover Ada (leaving), Maya (manager) Interviewer, Scribe, Buddy
payments-onboarding Ben (taking over), Maya Buddy, Scribe
  1. The Interviewer reads the system's folder first: code, cron file, runbook. Then it interviews Ada one question at a time. It asks what she owns, the recurring jobs, how things break, access and contacts, open promises, and the "never do X" rules.
  2. The Scribe checks each answer against the files. It writes HANDOVER.md, where every fact has a source: "(Ada, interview)" or "(ops/crontab:3)". Anything nobody confirmed goes under Open questions. Nothing is guessed.
  3. Maya, the manager, reads the guide in chat, asks for changes and replies "approve".
  4. Only then does the Scribe publish the guide as a room document in Ben's room.
  5. The Buddy answers Ben's questions from the guide. If the guide has no answer, it asks Ada in the other room, brings her reply back to Ben and tells the Scribe to update the guide.

The sample system is a small, made-up payments sync (workspace/ledger-sync). It has
the kind of gaps real systems have: a month-end job the runbook marks TODO, a hard-coded
FX fallback rate and a rate-limit workaround nobody wrote down.

Why Switch

Switch connects coding agents like Claude Code,
Codex and OpenCode to normal chat rooms. Five Switch features carry this project:

  • Templates: one YAML file creates all three agents, both rooms, a room group, the links between the rooms and the first message in each room.
  • @mentions: people and agents talk by mentioning each other in a normal Mattermost channel. Slack, Teams, Discord and Telegram work the same way.
  • Linked rooms: the Buddy can carry a question from Ben's room to Ada's room and back.
  • Room documents: the approved guide is a document attached to the onboarding room, so everyone there reads the same text.
  • Working directories: all three agents run inside the system's folder, so the Scribe can cite a file and line instead of trusting the interview.

Setting it up from zero

You need Docker and an agent provider.

1. Switch Console and a local server

Download Switch Console from the
releases page and choose
Run a local server. Console starts the Switch server and a Mattermost instance in Docker
on your machine, so you don't need a Slack workspace to try it.

Two Linux tips that cost me time:

  • Mattermost might not be on port 8065. Console picks free ports. Read the real one from ~/.config/switchdash/local-switch-server/ports.json.
  • Secret storage. On a Linux machine without a desktop keyring, Console warns that secure storage is unavailable. Installing gnome-keyring and starting Console with --password-store=gnome-libsecret fixed it.

2. An agent provider

I used OpenCode with Kimi K2.6 on Nebius Token Factory. Any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint works the same way. This is ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:

{
  "provider": {
    "nebius": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "https://api.tokenfactory.nebius.com/v1/",
        "apiKey": "{env:OPENAI_API_KEY}"
      },
      "models": { "moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6": { "name": "Kimi K2.6" } }
    }
  },
  "model": "nebius/moonshotai/Kimi-K2.6"
}

Export your key as OPENAI_API_KEY before starting Console. The key stays in your
environment and never goes into the file. Claude Code or Codex also work: pick them under
Advanced when you use the template.

3. Users

You need one person for each role. For a demo, create them in the local Mattermost:

C=$(docker ps --format '{{.Names}}' | grep mattermost)
for u in ada ben maya; do
  docker exec $C mmctl --local user create --username $u --email $u@example.com --password "<choose one>"
  docker exec $C mmctl --local team users add switch $u
done

4. The template

In Console, open Templates → Import template, pick
templates/handover.template.yaml,
then Use template. The form comes from the template's params: a name for the
handover, the three people, the system folder and the chat app. The preview on the right
shows what will be created.

The rooms and links part of the template is short:

rooms:
  - name: "{slug}-handover"
    agents: ["{slug}-interviewer", "{slug}-scribe", "{slug}-buddy"]
    users: ["{$creator}", "{leaver}", "{manager}"]
    kickoff: |
      @{slug}-interviewer @{leaver} is leaving and hands {slug} over to
      @{successor}. Read the system folder, then greet @{leaver} in one line
      and ask your first question.
  - name: "{slug}-onboarding"
    agents: ["{slug}-buddy", "{slug}-scribe"]
    users: ["{$creator}", "{successor}", "{manager}"]

links:
  - { from: "{slug}-onboarding", to: "{slug}-handover", label: interview with the leaver }
  - { from: "{slug}-handover", to: "{slug}-onboarding", label: successor's room }

Most of the work is in each agent's instructions, which are plain English. Click
Create all, and the Interviewer greets the leaver within seconds.

5. Run it

Sign in to Mattermost as ada and answer the questions. Sign in as maya to review the
guide, and as ben to ask the Buddy things. If you want to replay a run,
scripts/mm.py
posts and reads messages as any user through the Mattermost API.

What I learned

An agent only sees messages that mention it. This caught me during the recorded demo.
The Interviewer posted its notes as plain messages, without @payments-scribe in front.
It finished with "interview complete", and the Scribe never woke up. The instructions said
"tell the scribe", which isn't the same as "start the message with @payments-scribe". The
fix was to spell it out and give the reason: "post a note that starts with
@{slug}-scribe (the scribe only sees messages that mention it)".

Name the role, not just the person. In one run, the Scribe asked Ada to approve her own
guide, probably because she was the last person who had talked to it. Changing "ask @{manager}" to
"ask @{manager} (the manager, not the leaver)" fixed it. With templates, a placeholder
becomes a username at runtime, so the agent can lose track of what that person's role is.

"Read the folder first" is the most useful line in the template. Because the
Interviewer reads the code before it asks anything, its first question already names the
system: "You own ledger-sync — who else depends on it staying healthy?" The Scribe also
caught a gap Ada never mentioned: the month-end section of the runbook still says TODO.

Make the agent cite sources. Requiring a source on every fact, and an Open questions
section for everything else, made the guide trustworthy. It also gave the Buddy a clear
rule: if the answer isn't in the guide, don't make one up, ask Ada.

Approval should be a real gate. The Scribe publishes only after the manager replies
"approve" in chat. Maya's change ("make Ben the owner of the token rotation") shows up
in the guide before it reaches Ben.

Try it

Clone the repo, import the template and point System folder at workspace/ledger-sync,
or at a real system you're about to hand over. The full transcript of a run is in
examples/transcript.md
and the guide it produced is in
examples/HANDOVER.md.

HowISwitch

articles.title: Where Claude's usage limits went: from SSE to protobuf frames
articles.description: I maintain Claude Monitor, an open-source browser extension that shows claude.ai's usage limits: the...
articles.body_html:
I maintain Claude Monitor, an open-source browser extension that shows claude.ai's usage limits: the rolling 5-hour session and the weekly limit, with their reset times. It gets those numbers from two places, and in October one of them changed shape. This post covers what changed, how the extension reads the new format, what it leaves alone, and two quirks of the older source that matter if you build anything on these numbers.

None of this is a documented API. Everything below comes from my own accounts and from the extension's source, and it describes claude.ai as of mid-October 2026.

Two sources for the same numbers

The first source is the JSON endpoint behind claude.ai's usage settings page:

GET https://claude.ai/api/organizations/{org_id}/usage

It returns one object per limit (five_hour, seven_day and the per-model weekly caps), each with a utilization and a resets_at. Since around July 2026 it also returns a limits array, which is what the settings page renders. On paid plans this endpoint is all you need. On Free accounts it answers with every field set to null (I first saw that in August 2026), so for Free the limits have to come from somewhere else.

The second source is the reply itself. When a reply finishes, claude.ai sends the current limit windows along with it. On Free this is the only place the numbers show up. On paid plans the extension uses it mostly as a signal that a reply just finished, so it knows when to read /usage again.

Two quirks of /usage

utilization is a whole number. It comes back as an integer from 0 to 100. Light use reads 0 for a long stretch, and a chart of it moves in steps. Anything that estimates a rate from it needs several points of movement before the estimate means much.

resets_at jitters. Each read returns a slightly different reset time for the same window, sometimes earlier and sometimes later, on every bucket at once. These are the deltas I measured between consecutive polls on August 1, 2026:

+0.051 s   -0.274 s   -0.018 s   +0.909 s   -1.088 s

The window itself doesn't move; this is noise. But code that reads "the reset time changed" as "a new window started" fires on every poll. I shipped exactly that bug: the extension's history sampler compared reset times for inequality, saw a new window on every poll, and wrote a sample every 5 minutes instead of at most one every 10 (fixed in v1.12.2).

The fix is to define a rollover as the previous window having ended:

// prev and next are stored samples; reset times are epoch ms and next.t is "now".
function resetWindowChanged(prev, next) {
  return HISTORY_BUCKETS.some((key) => {
    const before = Number(prev?.buckets?.[key]?.reset ?? NaN);
    const after  = Number(next.buckets[key].reset ?? NaN);
    if (!Number.isFinite(before) || !Number.isFinite(after)) return false;
    return after > before && before <= next.t;
  });
}

For alerts that should fire once per window, the extension keeps the first reset time it saw as the window's id and treats any reset within 60 seconds of it as the same window. Keeping the stored id, instead of overwriting it on each poll, stops the jitter from adding up.

Before: server-sent events

In the classic chat interface, each reply is a POST to

/api/organizations/{org_id}/chat_conversations/{chat_id}/completion

answered with text/event-stream. Near the end of the stream there is one data: line with the limits. Its shape, trimmed:

data: {"type":"message_limit","message_limit":{..., "windows":{"5h":{"status":..., "resets_at":<unix seconds>, "utilization":<0 to 1>}, "7d":{...}}}}

The units differ from /usage: here utilization is a fraction from 0 to 1, and resets_at is a Unix timestamp in seconds instead of an ISO string. One more detail: a window that has run out reports "status": "exceeded_limit" while its utilization can still be below 1, so the extension shows 100% for that status instead of trusting the number.

The extension finds that line without decoding the rest of the stream. It splits the bytes on newlines, and only a line that starts with data: and contains the bytes "message_limit" gets turned into text and parsed.

After: Connect frames on StreamTimeline

In claude.ai's newer interface, which my Max account had by October 14, there is no /completion request. Sending a message is a POST to

/claudeai-rpc/anthropic.bard.api.v1alpha.ConversationService/PerformAction

and the reply arrives on a separate stream:

/claudeai-rpc/anthropic.bard.api.v1alpha.ConversationService/StreamTimeline
content-type: application/connect+proto

The first public report of this that I found was issue #59 on she-llac/claude-counter, opened on October 11.

This is the streaming format of the Connect protocol. The body is a sequence of frames, each with a 5-byte header (one flag byte and a 4-byte big-endian length) followed by the payload. Flag 0x01 means the payload is compressed, and 0x02 marks the end-of-stream frame, which carries JSON metadata.

What I saw: the reply's content comes in compressed frames, and the limits come in one small uncompressed frame, 119 bytes including the header. Decoded without a schema, its payload looks like this:

1 {
  10 { 1: "1791954046103-0" }
  11: 1
  4 {
    1: 1
    5: 0
    6: "org_level_disabled"
    9: "five_hour"
    13 { 1: "5h"  2 { 1: 1  2 { 1: 1791969600 }  3: 0.33 } }
    13 { 1: "7d"  2 { 1: 1  2 { 1: 1792404000 }  3: 0.24 } }
  }
}

The limit windows are the two field-13 entries. These are the bytes of the first one:

6a 19                             field 13, length-delimited, 25 bytes
   0a 02 35 68                    field 1: "5h"
   12 13                          field 2, 19 bytes
      08 01                       field 1: 1
      12 06                       field 2, 6 bytes
         08 c0 92 bd d6 06        field 1: 1791969600 (2026-10-14 09:20:00 UTC)
      19 1f 85 eb 51 b8 1e d5 3f  field 3, double: 0.33

My reading, which is inference and not documentation: field 13 is what a protobuf map<string, Window> looks like on the wire (each entry is a small message with the key in field 1 and the value in field 2), and {1: 1791969600} is a google.protobuf.Timestamp whose nanos is zero and therefore left out. So the JSON windows object seems to have become a map with the same "5h" and "7d" keys, each holding a status, a timestamp and the utilization as a double from 0 to 1. I don't use the other fields.

A few things follow for a parser:

  • proto3 does not serialize a double equal to 0. A window at 0%, such as a weekly window that has just reset, arrives without field 3, so a missing utilization next to a valid reset means 0, not "unknown".
  • In this frame both utilizations are still whole percentages (0.33 and 0.24), so the double adds no resolution over /usage. Both resets also fall on a round minute, with no sub-second noise. That's a single captured frame, so I can't say yet whether the stream's reset times jitter the way /usage's do.
  • The path says v1alpha. Field numbers can change without notice.

How the extension reads it

The reader is extension/page/stream.js, about 450 lines with no dependencies. It only runs after you turn on the extension's on-page bar. The extension then registers it with chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts in the page's MAIN world at document_start, so it wraps window.fetch before claude.ai's own code runs:

const previousFetch = window.fetch; // chain onto whatever is installed now

window.fetch = function (input, init) {
  const pending = previousFetch.apply(this, arguments);
  const kind = classify(input); // same origin and one of three path patterns, else null
  if (!kind) return pending;
  return pending.then((response) => {
    const scan = scannerFor(kind, response.headers.get('content-type') || '');
    if (scan) scan(response.clone()).catch(() => {}); // read a copy in the background
    return response;                                  // the page gets the original
  });
};

(The real wrapper also notes when a PerformAction request goes out, by its URL, and returns right away without touching it.)

The frame loop reads each 5-byte header and decides from the flags alone:

const flags = head[0];
const length = head[1] * 0x1000000 + (head[2] << 16) + (head[3] << 8) + head[4];
if (length > MAX_FRAME) { reader.cancel().catch(() => {}); return; } // 4 MB
if (flags & 0x02) { skip = length; continue; }                  // end of stream: not read
if (flags & 0x01) { sawReply = true; skip = length; continue; } // compressed: dropped unread
if (flags !== 0x00) { skip = length; continue; }
frame = { length };                                              // plain frame: collect it

A skipped frame is dropped from a queue of incoming chunks by its length, so a compressed frame is never decompressed or even joined into one buffer.

For plain frames the parser does not rely on field numbers, since an alpha API can renumber them. It works in three steps:

  1. A quick test on the raw bytes: does the payload contain 0x02 '5' 'h' or 0x02 '7' 'd', a length-2 field holding a label? If not, the frame is ignored.
  2. A schema-free walk that splits the bytes into fields by wire type and keeps only offsets. A window is any message that directly holds a 2-byte length-delimited field equal to "5h" or "7d".
  3. Inside a window, the utilization is the first double between 0 and 1.5, and the reset is the first integer that reads as a Unix time between one hour ago and eight days ahead. 
// Inside one window (its label already taken out of `list`)
for (const f of list) {
  if (f.wire === 1 && hit.utilization === null) {     // 64-bit field: a double
    const value = new DataView(bytes.buffer, bytes.byteOffset + f.start, 8).getFloat64(0, true);
    if (Number.isFinite(value) && value >= 0 && value <= 1.5) hit.utilization = value;
  } else if (f.wire === 0 && hit.resetsAt === null) { // varint: maybe a timestamp
    if (f.value > nowS - 3600 && f.value < nowS + RESET_AHEAD_S) hit.resetsAt = f.value;
  } else if (f.wire === 2 && depth < MAX_DEPTH) {     // nested message: look inside
    const sub = fields(bytes, f.start, f.end);
    if (sub) collect(bytes, sub, depth + 1, hit, nowS);
  }
}

One more wrinkle. A stream that reopens, for example after a reload, can replay the timeline, limits frame included, without anything being sent. Opening a chat from the sidebar fires a PerformAction of its own, although in my captures that stream carried no limits frame. To count messages, the extension treats a limits frame as a new reply only when a PerformAction request from the same page came first and compressed reply frames followed it. It also keeps a short FNV-1a hash of each limits payload, so a replayed frame isn't reported twice.

What it does not read

  • Request bodies. A send is recognized by its URL only.
  • Compressed frames, which carry the reply. Only their 5-byte header is read.
  • Any other byte as text. In the protobuf path, labels are compared as bytes and only numbers come out. In the SSE path, the one data: line that contains "message_limit" is decoded as JSON. The only body parsed whole is the small JSON error claude.ai returns instead of a stream when a send is refused at the limit; it carries the same limit payload and no conversation content.
  • Anything past 8 MB per response or 4 MB per frame: reading stops there.

What leaves the script is the utilization and reset time of the two windows, plus a little bookkeeping (the frame hash, and whether a send came first). It goes by window.postMessage, same origin, to the extension's own content script on the page, then to its service worker, which keeps it in chrome.storage.local. For a messages-left estimate it stores the time, utilization and frame hash of the last 20 replies.

One caveat, to be clear about where these limits come from: they are a property of the code, not of the browser. A script in the page's main world can see whatever the page fetches, and Chrome's warning for the extension says "Read and change your data on claude.ai" because host permissions can't be narrowed to paths. The source is unminified with no build step, and each release has GPG-signed checksums, so you can check that what you installed matches the repository. SECURITY.md has the details, including a console snippet that shows what Chrome actually grants.

What I haven't verified

  • I verified the new transport with a Max account only. My Free test account was still on the classic interface when I tested on October 14, and there the SSE path works. I don't know yet whether Free accounts on the new interface get the same limits frame. If you have one and the numbers look wrong, an issue with what you see would help.
  • The protobuf layout comes from one captured frame plus live tests on one account.
  • Field meanings beyond the labels, the timestamp and the double are guesses.

If you parse these numbers yourself

  • Compare reset times with a tolerance, and detect a new window by the old reset having passed, not by the value changing.
  • Expect whole percentages from both sources.
  • On StreamTimeline, anchor on what you can recognize (the "5h" and "7d" labels and plausible values) rather than on field numbers, and treat a missing double as 0.
  • If you only need the limits, skip compressed frames by their length. There is no need to decompress the reply.

The extension

Claude Monitor shows the 5-hour session, the weekly limit, per-model weekly caps and extra-usage credits in a toolbar popup, with reset countdowns and alerts at thresholds you choose. The on-page bar described above is optional. Version 1.21.0, which reads both transports, is out for Chrome, Firefox and Edge. It's MIT-licensed and not affiliated with Anthropic.

  • Chrome: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/bfhdcfiigpaaopklllpobkheakpigbfo?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=sse-to-protobuf-2026-10
  • Firefox: https://addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/claude-usage-meter/
  • Edge: https://microsoftedge.microsoft.com/addons/detail/ilidbhklkpefboidlfeoiiacepcefinp
  • Source: https://github.com/claude-monitor/claude-monitor-browser-extension

The extension itself only talks to claude.ai and has no analytics. The one thing the project receives is an optional uninstall survey, described in the privacy policy.

articles.title: Tiny image placeholders with sharp: bytes for 8 to 32 px LQIPs
articles.description: A 16 px WebP placeholder of a 576.8 KB photo is 108 bytes, 167 characters as a data URI. Bytes for 8 to 32 px in four formats, measured with sharp.
articles.body_html:
A blurred placeholder only needs to be 16 pixels wide, and as WebP it costs about 100 bytes. With sharp, a 16 × 11 WebP of a 1920 × 1280 photo came out at 108 bytes, or 167 characters as a data URI you can inline in your HTML. At 32 px it is 248 bytes. Format matters more than width at this size: the same 16 px placeholder is 330 bytes as JPEG and 600 bytes as PNG.

How do you make one?

Resize to a tiny width, encode, and base64 the buffer:

import sharp from 'sharp';

const src = 'jpg-sample-photo-original.jpg';
console.log('width  format  bytes  base64 chars  data URI chars');
for (const w of [8, 16, 24, 32]) {
  for (const [fmt, opts] of [['webp', { quality: 50 }], ['jpeg', { quality: 50 }], ['png', { compressionLevel: 9 }], ['avif', { quality: 50 }]]) {
    const buf = await sharp(src).resize(w).toFormat(fmt, opts).toBuffer();
    const b64 = buf.toString('base64');
    const uri = `data:image/${fmt};base64,${b64}`;
    console.log(String(w).padEnd(6), fmt.padEnd(7), String(buf.length).padEnd(6), String(b64.length).padEnd(13), uri.length);
  }
}

resize(w) keeps the aspect ratio, so the four sizes came out at 8 × 5, 16 × 11, 24 × 16 and 32 × 21.

How many bytes does each size cost?

What the script printed:

width  format  bytes  base64 chars  data URI chars
8      webp    78     104           127
8      jpeg    292    392           415
8      png     211    284           306
8      avif    300    400           423
16     webp    108    144           167
16     jpeg    330    440           463
16     png     600    800           822
16     avif    344    460           483
24     webp    188    252           275
24     jpeg    375    500           523
24     png     1162   1552          1574
24     avif    360    480           503
32     webp    248    332           355
32     jpeg    457    612           635
32     png     1928   2572          2594
32     avif    446    596           619

The same numbers as a data URI, which is what lands in your HTML:

Width WebP JPEG AVIF PNG
8 px 127 415 423 306
16 px 167 463 483 822
24 px 275 523 503 1,574
32 px 355 635 619 2,594

Why does WebP win at this size?

Container overhead. A JPEG carries quantization and Huffman tables before the first pixel; at 8 px that header is much of the 292 bytes. AVIF wraps its data in an ISO box structure that costs a few hundred bytes too. A lossy WebP's RIFF header is 20 bytes or so, and the rest is picture.

PNG goes the other way. It is lossless, so every one of the 32 × 21 pixels is stored exactly, and the photo's noise makes that expensive: 1,928 bytes at 32 px.

Note: base64 grows bytes by a third, and the data:image/webp;base64, prefix adds 23 characters. Compare placeholders by the data URI length if you inline them, not by the file size. A 600-byte PNG is 822 characters in your HTML.

How small can you go before it stops helping?

The placeholders, stretched to 360 × 240 with a blur the way a page shows them:

At 8 px you get the colour and a light patch in the middle, and nothing more. At 16 px the iguana's shape and the branch appear. At 24 and 32 px the shape sharpens a little, for 80 and 140 more bytes than 16 px. For most layouts 16 px is the point where you stop paying for detail nobody waits to see.

What about a single colour?

A flat colour is cheaper still: no bytes beyond your CSS. But pick it carefully. sharp's stats().dominant returned { r: 8, g: 8, b: 8 } for this photo, near black, because the dark background has the most pixels. The iguana is orange.

Two better choices from the same file:

const { channels } = await sharp(src).stats();
console.log(channels.map((c) => Math.round(c.mean)));      // [ 67, 54, 26 ]

const { data } = await sharp(src).resize(1, 1).raw().toBuffer({ resolveWithObject: true });
console.log([...data]);                                     // [ 81, 59, 28 ]

The channel mean and a 1 × 1 resize both give a dark olive brown, which matches the photo's overall tone. Use one of them as a background-color when a 167-character URI is still too much, for example in a long grid of cards.

How do you use it on the page?

Inline the URI as a background on the image box, and let the real image cover it:

<img
  src="iguana-1200.webp"
  width="1920" height="1280"
  loading="lazy"
  alt="An iguana on a branch"
  style="background: url(data:image/webp;base64,UklGRmQAAABXRUJQVlA4IFgAAADwAQCdASoQAAsAAsBMJaACdAEDHZBTWgAA/vkj8Bo1wNbZdUdcxmtM2/Tv4dDTBQ52v/GCf9yAu+CEHeT5yhIgSkX+3CJh5tSaDAboDe9Kb0zaqjfn+VAA) center / cover;">

That is the real 16 px placeholder from the run. The browser scales a tiny bitmap smoothly, which gives you most of the blur for free. Add filter: blur() on a wrapper if you want it softer, not on the <img> itself, or the real image blurs too.

Keep width and height on the image. The placeholder fills a box; the attributes are what reserve it before anything loads. For the rest of an image's journey to the page, the image optimization guide covers formats, sizing and lazy loading.

How I measured

  • Apple Silicon Mac (M1 Pro), 2026-10-17, Node 24.22.0, sharp 0.35.4 with libvips 8.18.6.
  • Source: jpg-sample-photo-original.jpg from the Blinkimg site, 1920 × 1280, 576,828 bytes, a real camera photo.
  • WebP, JPEG and AVIF at quality 50; PNG at compressionLevel: 9. Defaults otherwise.
  • The figure scales each placeholder to 360 × 240 with resize(..., { fit: 'fill' }).blur(6) in sharp; a browser's scaling will look a little different.

What I did not test

I did not compare BlurHash or ThumbHash strings, which need a client-side decoder. One photo with a dark background is not every photo.

I build Blinkimg, an image compressor and converter with a developer API. I wrote this article with help from an AI assistant (Claude), which ran the code on my machine; every number in it comes from those runs.
